title: Engineering 3'-UTR hairpin structures to modulate mRNA stability and recombinant protein production in Escherichia coli.
abstract: Engineering mRNA stability is a promising yet underexplored approach for improving recombinant protein production in bacterial systems. In this study, we evaluated the effect of synthetic 3'-UTR hairpin structures on mRNA stability and protein yield in Escherichia coli using two SUMO-fusion expression systems. Hairpin elements with defined structural features were introduced downstream of the coding sequence. In all constructs, 3'-UTR hairpins increased mRNA half-life, with stabilization ranging from approximately 2-fold to 3-fold (n = 3 biological replicates). In the SUMO-SARS-CoV-2-derived peptide system, enhanced transcript stability was accompanied by a marked increase in specific cellular fusion-protein content, reaching up to 6.8-fold relative to the control (n = 3). In the SUMO-liraglutide-derived peptide system, mRNA stabilization was also pronounced, and the increase in specific cellular fusion-protein content reached approximately 3-fold (p < 0.001, n = 6). These findings show that 3'-UTR engineering is an effective strategy for modulating mRNA stability in *E. coli*, but the quantitative relationship between transcript persistence and protein accumulation is context-dependent and likely influenced by additional factors, including translation efficiency. Overall, engineering of 3'-terminal RNA structures provides a practical tool for post-transcriptional tuning of recombinant expression systems.

title: Rethinking endpoints for anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with hr+ early breast cancer receiving endocrine therapy: from body weight and BMI to body composition.
abstract: Body weight (BW) and body mass index (BMI) are commonly used to assess obesity and response to weight-management interventions in patients with hormone receptor-positive (HR+) early breast cancer (eBC) receiving endocrine therapy. However, these measures do not adequately reflect changes in fat mass, visceral adiposity, lean mass and sarcopenia-related phenotypes. This focused narrative review examines whether BW and BMI are sufficient endpoints for evaluating obesity management and anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with HR+ eBC receiving endocrine therapy. PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for relevant evidence until 23 June 2026, including BC-specific studies of obesity pharmacotherapy and registered interventional trials. Studies have reported increases in total and visceral fat mass after adjuvant BC treatment, while changes in lean mass have been less consistent. The identified BC-specific studies remain mainly retrospective and weight-centric, with none assessing body composition as a key outcome. BW and BMI may be useful entry and monitoring variables, but insufficient as stand-alone endpoints. Body composition should be considered as a complementary endpoint, alongside metabolic, functional and oncologic outcomes. Future studies should also assess endocrine therapy adherence and persistence to better characterize the benefits and risks of anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with HR+ eBC.

title: Persistence and geographic availability of Medicare Part D coverage for non-diabetes GLP-1 therapies, 2024-2026.
From Satiety to Reward Reshaping: Central Mechanisms of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Therapeutic Implications for Reward-related Disorders.
abstract: The classical theory of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) emphasizes peripheral metabolic regulation and satiety mediated by hypothalamic-brainstem homeostatic pathways. However, numerous clinical studies have shown that GLP-1RAs significantly suppress patients' food cravings and simultaneously reduce cravings for non-food reinforcers such as alcohol and nicotine, suggesting that the effects of GLP-1RAs extend far beyond the regulation of energy balance. GLP-1 receptors are expressed in the ventral tegmental area, the nucleus accumbens, and the central amygdala; their activation exhibits phase-specific effects: during the reward anticipation phase, they reduce dopamine signaling in the nucleus accumbens, whereas during the intake phase, they enhance this signaling. GLP-1RAs can modulate the mesolimbic dopamine system, likely through a combination of direct central actions and indirect peripheral- to-central signaling pathways, dynamically modulating reward processing rather than simply inhibiting it. Given that the mesolimbic dopamine system serves as a common neural substrate for both food and drug addiction, the observed modulatory effects of GLP-1RAs on various reinforcers suggest preliminary potential for expanded application in the treatment of binge eating disorder and substance use disorders, although clinical evidence remains limited for most non-food indications. Future research should elucidate the central penetration characteristics of different agonists, their cell-type-specific mechanisms of action, and the persistence of their neuromodulatory effects to advance the development of precision therapeutic strategies targeting specific reward circuits.

title: Beyond Insulin Therapy: Therapeutic Potential of Alpha-glucosidase Inhibitors in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
abstract: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is a progressive autoimmune condition that destroys pancreatic β-cells, resulting in insulin deficiency and disruption of carbohydrate, protein, and fat metabolism. Although insulin therapy remains the cornerstone of T1DM management, achieving optimal glycaemic control can still be difficult due to hypoglycaemia, weight gain, and limitations in insulin pharmacodynamics. Therefore, adjunctive non-insulin therapies have been investigated to improve metabolic outcomes in T1DM. Among these adjunctive approaches, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (AGIs) offer a unique insulinindependent mechanism by delaying intestinal carbohydrate digestion and absorption, thereby attenuating postprandial glucose excursions. This review critically evaluates the pharmacological basis, clinical efficacy, safety profile, and therapeutic relevance of AGIs as adjunctive agents in T1DM. The available evidence suggests that AGIs may produce modest reductions in glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), improve postprandial glycaemic control, and potentially reduce insulin requirements; however, gastrointestinal adverse effects remain a major limitation to long-term treatment adherence. The efficacy of AGIs is also compared with that of other adjunctive therapies, including metformin, pramlintide, GLP-1 agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors, and SGLT-2 inhibitors. Although newer adjunctive therapies may offer broader metabolic benefits, AGIs may still have clinical utility in selected individuals with marked postprandial hyperglycaemia, high carbohydrate intake, or contraindications to alternative adjunctive agents. Further studies are required to define the role of AGIs in contemporary T1DM management, including the use of continuous glucose monitoring-derived metrics, long-term cardiovascular outcomes and personalized therapeutic strategies.

title: Tirzepatide for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea: from apnea-hypopnea index reduction to cardiometabolic risk mitigation-a narrative review.
abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic respiratory disorder with nocturnal oxygen desaturation that is often associated with multisystemic sequelae such as hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, and increased morbidity and mortality. Obesity has been proposed as a modifiable risk factor; hence, the recent shift in focus to investigating anti-obesity medications for the management of OSA. Tirzepatide is the first U.S. FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for the treatment of moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity to be utilized in combination with low caloric intake and physical activity, given its prior success in managing type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity. This narrative review evaluates tirzepatide and the SURMOUNT-OSA trial program as the key contemporary anchors for the pharmacological treatment of OSA in adults with concurrent obesity. Because the randomized evidence base currently comprises a single pivotal trial program, the review centers on SURMOUNT-OSA and its prespecified endpoints along with post hoc analyses, supplemented by observational, modeling, and mechanistic studies. In the SURMOUNT-OSA program, tirzepatide produced randomized, placebo-controlled reductions in the apnea-hypopnea index, sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, body weight, and systemic inflammation. The program was designed around respiratory and metabolic endpoints rather than clinical events, so it cannot support conclusions about mortality, cardiovascular, or renal outcomes. Favorable signals for those events, including all-cause mortality, major adverse kidney events, and major adverse cardiovascular events, come only from nonrandomized observational cohorts and are best regarded as directional and exploratory rather than definitive. Tirzepatide may help frame OSA as a multifactorial and partially metabolically treatable disease and may represent a clinically meaningful expansion of treatment options alongside, rather than as a replacement for, established mechanical and procedural therapies. The available evidence is anchored in a single phase 3 trial program and limited by short follow-up and the absence of definitive comparative and long-term outcome data. Long-term durability of effect after discontinuation, generalizability beyond the SURMOUNT-OSA-eligible population, OSA-specific economic analysis, and head-to-head comparisons against CPAP remain the principal unsettled questions requiring dedicated long-term studies before firm clinical recommendations can be made.

title: Beyond the Scale: Psychological and Behavioural Considerations Following GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Treatment Discontinuation.
The pharmacological frontier in obstructive sleep apnoea: From pathophysiologic endotypes to precision medicine.
journal: Lung India : official organ of Indian Chest Society
abstract: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea (OSA) is a prevalent global health crisis with limited real-world effectiveness of Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) due to suboptimal adherence. Modern understanding has shifted from a purely mechanical model to the PALM Scale, which identifies anatomical and non-anatomical endotypes: Pcrit (Anatomy), Arousal threshold, Loop gain and Muscle responsiveness. This review synthesises current pharmacological advances targeting these specific endotypes to provide alternatives for CPAP-intolerant patients. We analysed landmark clinical trials including SURMOUNT-OSA (Tirzepatide), SCALE (Liraglutide), FLOW TRIAL (Sulthiame) and MARIPOSA (AD109). This review showed Incretin-based therapies (e.g., Tirzepatide) produce large and clinically meaningful reductions in Apnoea-Hypopnea Index (AHI), often exceeding 40-50% in many patients. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., Sulthiame) stabilise ventilatory instability (Loop Gain), reducing AHI by approximately 40%. Combined noradrenergic-antimuscarinic agents (e.g., AD109) enhance upper airway muscle responsiveness. Furthermore, Solriamfetol and Pitolisant effectively manage residual daytime sleepiness in PAP-adherent patients. So the management of OSA is entering an era of Precision Medicine. Pharmacotherapy may serve as an adjunct to PAP, and in selected phenotypes, could function as a potential alternative option, particularly in the Indian 'thin-fat' phenotype (normal BMI with central adiposity and visceral fat), where CPAP adherence remains challenging.

title: Efficacy and safety of semaglutide versus placebo in adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes: updated meta-analysis of randomized trials.
journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
abstract: Obesity poses significant challenges for those seeking long-term weight loss through diet and exercise alone. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist approved for chronic weight management in eligible adults. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of semaglutide for treating obesity in adults without diabetes. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261338170). PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched through February 28, 2026. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing semaglutide with placebo in adults without diabetes with BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 or ≥ 27 kg/m2 and at least one obesity-related comorbidity. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 Tool, GRADE methodology, RevMan v5.4, and CMA v3 were used for risk-of-bias assessment, certainty-of-evidence assessment, data analyses, and meta-regression analyses respectively. We included 10 RCTs with a total of 7,131 participants. Risk-of-bias was judged at the level of each outcome: all included trials were at low risk-of-bias for the efficacy outcomes and the prespecified safety outcomes, while cardiovascular and psychiatric disorders raised some concerns. Compared to placebo, semaglutide produced significantly greater reductions in percentage change in body weight (WMD -12.29%, 95% CI -13.38 to -11.20, I2 88%, 95% PI -16.06 to -8.52; 10 studies, n = 6975), absolute change in body weight from baseline (WMD -12.67 kg, 95% CI -13.53 to -11.81, I2 77%, 95% PI -15.36 to -9.98; 10 studies, n = 6975), BMI (WMD -4.55 kg/m2, 95% CI -5.08 to -4.03, I2 86%, 95% PI -6.33 to -2.78; 8 studies, n = 6573), and waist circumference (WMD -9.42 cm, 95% CI -10.27 to -8.56, I2 79%, 95% PI -12.12 to -6.71; 10 studies, n = 6970). Participants assigned to semaglutide also had a higher probability of reaching a ≥ 5%, 10%, 15%, or 20% loss of body weight (9 studies, n = 6103). However, substantial between-study heterogeneity was observed for efficacy outcomes, indicating that the magnitude of benefit varied across trials. With semaglutide, individuals experienced a greater number of total adverse events (aggregate proportions 90.0% vs. 85.0%; RR 1.06, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.10, I2 72%; 9 studies, n = 6922) and discontinuation due to adverse events (aggregate proportions 6.0% vs. 3.0%; RR 1.86, 95% CI 1.41 to 2.45, I2 0%; 10 studies, n = 7129) than did individuals taking the placebo; while for serious adverse events (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.51, I2 40%; 10 studies, n = 7129) the estimate was imprecise, did not establish a clear difference and the interval remains compatible with a potentially important increase in risk. These pooled figures represent average effects and may not apply equally across different semaglutide doses, formulations, treatment duration, or patient populations. Certainty-of-evidence was low for the primary outcome of percentage change in body weight and for absolute change in body weight and change in BMI, and very low for change in waist circumference. Semaglutide was associated with clinically meaningful weight loss during trial treatment periods in adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes; however, low-certainty evidence and substantial between-study heterogeneity warrant cautious interpretation of the magnitude of benefit. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40200-026-02108-x.

title: Cultural adaptation of nutritional recommendations in the comprehensive care of adults with type 2 diabetes: An updated transcultural diabetes nutrition algorithm (tDNA) framework.
abstract: The transcultural Diabetes Nutrition Algorithm (tDNA) applies medical nutrition therapy (MNT) for adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D) by aligning evidence-based dietary principles with cultural food patterns, clinical workflows, and health-system realities. To review the evidence underpinning the tDNA framework, describe its role in culturally adapting MNT across current treatment contexts, and identify priorities for research, education, and implementation. Sources include concept and framework papers, regional adaptations, randomized and pragmatic evaluations of tDNA-aligned programs, clinician toolkit assessments, and practice statements. Evidence was abstracted around tDNA decision nodes: risk stratification, carbohydrate quality and distribution, portion guidance, meal timing, physical activity prompts, use of diabetes-specific formulas (DSFs) as a meal replacement or supplement when indicated, and digitally enabled monitoring. Regional tDNA adaptations for Asian Indian, Malaysian, Canadian, Middle Eastern, Brazilian and Venezuelan settings are expert consensus documents specifying culturally appropriate modifications. A published randomized controlled trial reports that calorie-prescribed, glycemic index/load-guided tDNA integrating DSFs and augmented by structured behavior counseling improves glycemic control and body weight over 6 to 12 months, with gains in eating self-efficacy supporting adherence. We propose that MNT as a co-therapy be aligned to dosing when pharmacotherapy is initiated. For the highly effective glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, culturally adapted standardized nutrition checkpoints are proposed to support nutritional adequacy. Whether structured nutrition therapy using DSFs preserves lean mass in this setting is an area for further research. The tDNA framework offers a structure for culturally adapted nutrition care in T2D. We propose its extension to current pharmacotherapy and digitally enabled delivery; these extensions require prospective evaluation. Recommendations include early localization, integration with drug titration, structured nutrition support where indicated, standardized nutrition checkpoints, digitized implementation, and audit of remission, time in range, weight, and adherence.

title: Efficacy and safety of oral orforglipron in Japanese participants with obesity disease (ATTAIN-J): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase 3 trial.
abstract: Orforglipron, a small-molecule, non-peptide, oral GLP-1 receptor agonist, has shown bodyweight reduction and cardiometabolic benefits in adults with obesity across phase 3 trials globally. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of orforglipron versus placebo for treating obesity disease in Japanese adults. ATTAIN-J was a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase 3 trial conducted across 16 medical research centres and hospitals in Japan and included adults aged 18 years or older with a BMI between 27 kg/m2 and less than 35 kg/m2 and two or more obesity-related health disorders, or a BMI of 35 kg/m2 or higher and one or more obesity-related health disorder, with one or more of the obesity-related health disorders being hypertension, dyslipidaemia, or type 2 diabetes (targeted at about 25% of participants), consistent with Japanese indications for tirzepatide and semaglutide for obesity disease; and at least one unsuccessful dietary attempt to lose weight. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) via a computer-generated sequence to once-daily oral orforglipron (6 mg, 12 mg, or 36 mg) or placebo. Co-primary endpoints were mean percentage change in bodyweight and percentage of participants with at least 5% bodyweight reduction from baseline to week 72. Efficacy endpoints were primarily evaluated by the treatment regimen estimand in all randomly assigned participants. Safety was assessed in participants who received at least one dose of study treatment. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05931380 (completed). Between July 31, 2023, and June 19, 2025, 291 participants were screened, of whom 238 (144 [61%] males and 94 [39%] females; mean age 54·1 years [SD 11·2]) were randomly assigned to receive orforglipron 6 mg (n=61), 12 mg (n=57), or 36 mg (n=60), or placebo (n=60); 214 (90%) participants completed the study. At week 72, mean percentage change in bodyweight was -5·9% (95% CI -7·6 to -4·2) with orforglipron 6 mg, -8·7% (-10·9 to -6·5) with 12 mg, and -7·9% (-10·0 to -5·8) with 36 mg, compared with -0·6% (-2·1 to 0·8) with placebo (all p<0·0001 vs placebo). At week 72, a bodyweight reduction of at least 5% was seen in 15·2% (SE 4·8; nine of 60) of participants in the placebo group compared with 45·6% (6·1; 28 of 61; p=0·0001) of participants in the orforglipron 6 mg group, 60·8% (6·4; 35 of 57; p<0·0001) of participants in the orforglipron 12 mg group, and 58·8% (6·5; 35 of 60; p<0·0001) of participants in the orforglipron 36 mg group. Adverse events with orforglipron were mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal symptoms. Across all orforglipron groups, treatment-emergent adverse events that most frequently led to study treatment discontinuation were nausea (one [2%] of 61 in the 6 mg group, one [2%] of 57 in the 12 mg group, and five [8%] of 60 in the 36 mg group vs none with placebo) and vomiting (none in the 6 mg group, two [4%] in the 12 mg group, and one [2%] in the 36 mg group vs none in the placebo group). In Japanese adults with obesity disease, once-daily orforglipron resulted in statistically superior reductions in bodyweight versus placebo, with a safety profile consistent with that of other GLP-1 receptor agonists. Eli Lilly and Company. For the Japanese translation of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section.

title: From metabolic therapy to addiction care: a clinical pharmacology roadmap for GLP-1 receptor agonists in substance use disorders.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), established treatments for type 2 diabetes and obesity, are being investigated for substance use disorders (SUDs). Randomized evidence is emerging in alcohol use disorder (AUD), while evidence for opioid, nicotine, cocaine, cannabis, and stimulant use disorders remains mixed, observational, or investigational. This targeted narrative review integrates PubMed/MEDLINE literature, US Food and Drug Administration guidance and labeling, and ClinicalTrials.gov records available through 15 July 2026, with targeted literature and registry updates through 20 October 2026. It evaluates mechanistic plausibility, randomized and real-world human evidence, agent- and dose-specific pharmacology, co-treatment with established SUD medications, safety, adherence, benefit-risk assessment, harm reduction, equity, and trial design. The evidence is sufficient to justify indication-specific clinical development, especially for AUD, but currently insufficient for routine off-label treatment of SUDs for patients without an approved metabolic indication. Near-term research should test GLP-1 RAs as adjuncts rather than replacements for established SUD care, distinguish direct reward effects from weight loss and adverse-effect pathways, and embed risk minimization, patient-important outcomes, and equitable access into development from the outset.

title: The pharmacist's role in enhancing adherence to GLP1 based anti-obesity medications through comprehensive side effect management.
journal: Exploratory research in clinical and social pharmacy
abstract: The emergence of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP1) and GLP1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonists (hereinafter GLP1-RAs, GLP1-GIP-RAs) have transformed obesity treatment. These agents offer substantial weight loss and notable cardiometabolic and other health benefits. Yet, their success relies on long-term adherence and careful management of side effects. Common adverse events - especially gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances - often lead to treatment discontinuation, weight regain and reduced effectiveness. As healthcare providers with multiple patients' interactions, pharmacists provide continuous care throughout the entire treatment journey, from initiation through titration phase and long-term maintenance. The unique position of pharmacists' interactions with patients enables them to address the high rates of non-adherence commonly observed with GLP1 based medications, which often stem from GI side effects, medication complexity, and patient education gaps. Treatment persistence and patient outcomes can be significantly improved through structured, pharmacist-led strategies, including comprehensive patient education, lifestyle modifications, and judicious use of over-the-counter interventions and vitamin/mineral/supplement therapies. Critical emphasis is placed on the pharmacist's role in preventing and managing serious complications associated with rapid weight loss, particularly sarcopenia and nutrient deficiencies, while maintaining vigilance for "red flags" that signal serious complications requiring physician intervention. This manuscript delineates the rationale for pharmacist involvement through the phases of adherence: initiation, titration, persistence, and discontinuation. It provides side-effect incidence and management tables, possible lifestyle and treatment options in each phase, red-flag and referral criteria, strategies to prevent sarcopenia and nutrient deficiency. Implementing these pharmacist-driven interventions can significantly improve tolerability, adherence, and long-term clinical outcomes in obesity pharmacotherapy.

title: Early Treatment Trajectory and Long-Term Persistence to Semaglutide for Obesity: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
abstract: To assess semaglutide persistence in obesity management, identify factors associated with discontinuation and examine early tirzepatide adoption. This retrospective cohort study used Clalit Health Services records of adults without diabetes initiating Wegovy between January and May 2025. Discontinuation was defined as a gap exceeding 60 days after medication coverage ended. Multivariable Cox models, including a Day-90 landmark analysis, assessed discontinuation. Tirzepatide adoption was evaluated following its December 2025 coverage introduction. Among 34 309 participants (67.0% women; mean age 44.6 years), cumulative discontinuation reached 36.5% at 180 days and 67.6% at 365 days. Arab population sector (hazard ratio [HR] 1.65, 95% CI 1.59-1.72), low socioeconomic status (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.09-1.17) and current smoking (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.09-1.17) were associated with discontinuation. In the day-90 landmark cohort (n = 28 218), remaining on 0.25 versus 1.0 mg was associated with subsequent discontinuation (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.72-2.06), substantially attenuated after adjustment for early refill adherence. Each percentage-point smaller BMI reduction was associated with 3% higher discontinuation hazard (HR 1.03, 95% CI 1.03-1.04). Following tirzepatide availability, 2908 of 33 936 eligible participants (8.6%) initiated treatment over a median 3.1-month observation period. Adoption was associated with higher socioeconomic status and baseline BMI. Semaglutide discontinuation was common and associated with sociodemographic and early treatment characteristics. Day-90 dose and early weight-loss response may help identify discontinuation risk. Socioeconomic differences suggest inequalities in sustained obesity pharmacotherapy access.

title: Research progress on bowel preparation regimens before colonoscopy: a narrative review.
abstract: Adequate bowel preparation is the single most important determinant of colonoscopy quality, yet suboptimal preparation affects up to one-quarter of colonoscopies, leading to repeat procedures, increased health-system costs, and health disparities. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence on bowel preparation regimens through a public health lens, organized around four interconnected dimensions: cleansing efficacy, safety, tolerability, and population-specific applicability. We define and classify preparation regimens by volume (high-volume ≥4 L, low-volume 2-<4 L, ultra-low-volume <2 L) and administration schedule (split-dose, same-day). Low-volume, split-dose formulations achieve non-inferior cleansing efficacy to high-volume 4L polyethylene glycol (PEG) regimens, with improved patient tolerability and compliance. The Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (BBPS) is the most widely adopted assessment instrument; commonly used adequate preparation is defined as total BBPS ≥6 with each segment ≥2, although definitions vary across studies. PEG-based preparations maintain the most favorable safety profile, particularly in patients with renal or cardiovascular comorbidities, while sodium phosphate carries a small but clinically significant risk of acute phosphate nephropathy. Special populations-including older adults with frailty and polypharmacy, patients with inflammatory bowel disease, and those with diabetes-require tailored preparation strategies. Emerging evidence on glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), linaclotide, simethicone, dietary optimization, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based bowel preparation assessment is critically evaluated. Health system implications, including the impact of inadequate preparation on resource utilization, adherence barriers linked to health literacy, and equity considerations, are examined. The review concludes that no single regimen is universally optimal; personalized preparation strategies integrating risk stratification, AI-assisted quality assessment, and evidence-based adjunctive protocols represent the most promising path toward improving colonoscopy outcomes at the population level.

title: Obesity Medications in Older Adults: A Geriatrics 5Ms Framework for Safe and Patient-Centered Prescribing.
journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
abstract: Obesity medications that act through gut-derived hormonal pathways include glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1), dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1/GIP), and emerging triple glucagon-like peptide-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon receptor agonists. These therapies are increasingly prescribed for weight management and glycemic control, as well as for their cardiometabolic and renal benefits. While these medications offer substantial benefits to patients across multiple health conditions, their use in older adults warrants heightened scrutiny. Older adults face increased risks of sarcopenia and frailty, and evidence from major clinical trials suggests that a substantial proportion of medication-associated weight loss agents may result in loss of lean mass, potentially posing risks for this population. Other adverse effects that may be more consequential in older adults include dehydration, malnutrition, perioperative aspiration, and fat-predominant weight regain after discontinuation. This paper provides a clinically oriented framework to guide prescribing decisions for older adults. Drawing on patient scenarios from common geriatric contexts, including frailty, cognitive impairment, glucocorticoid use, and surgical planning, we propose prescribing approaches that optimize therapeutic benefits while mitigating potential harms. We integrate these recommendations within the Geriatrics 5Ms Framework (Mind, Mobility, Medications, Multicomplexity, and Matters Most) to contextualize treatment within geriatrics practice. Lifestyle co-interventions, particularly resistance training, adequate protein intake, and ongoing functional monitoring, emerge as essential components for older adults receiving these therapies. We also discuss identifying priority areas for future research, including age-stratified clinical trials and the routine inclusion of body composition and physical function outcomes.

title: Continued CagriSema treatment preserves weight loss by reducing energy intake and maintaining energy expenditure in rats.
abstract: CagriSema (CS), combining the amylin receptor agonist cagrilintide with the glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist semaglutide, is being developed for obesity and type 2 diabetes. We quantified CS effects on energy balance during initial treatment, weight maintenance, and after discontinuation. Male diet-induced obese rats underwent indirect calorimetry during 6 weeks of treatment and for 4 weeks after discontinuation. Treatments were a) vehicle, b) CS, c) calorie-restriction to match CS body weight loss (weight matched, WM), and d) calorie-restriction to match CS food intake (pair-feeding, PF). CS effects occurred in four phases. During days 1-10 (Phase I), CS induced rapid weight loss mainly through reduced energy intake (EI), while energy expenditure (EE) was relatively preserved. EE was significantly lower in WM rats, consistent with metabolic adaptation. During days 11-42 (Phase II), reduced body weight was maintained in the CS, WM, and PF groups, and respiratory exchange ratio converged across groups, indicating metabolic steady state had been reached. Reduced EI and preserved total EE respectively explained 86% and 14% of CS weight loss efficacy. Maintained resting/sleeping EE contributed to the total EE preservation. Treatment discontinuation (days 43-52, Phase III) caused hyperphagia and rapid weight regain. During days 53-68 (Phase IV), all groups reached metabolic steady state and weight gain returned to pretreatment rates. Body weight plateaued in approximately half the time needed to reach metabolic steady state, and metabolic adaptation reversed within ∼7 days after discontinuation. By persistently lowering EI and attenuating metabolic adaptation, CS enables sustained weight loss in rats; however, the reversal after treatment cessation suggests that chronic pharmacological therapy may be required to maintain weight loss.

title: The Impact of Incretin-Based Therapies on Anthropometric and Metabolic Parameters in Women with Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), recently renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), affects 170 million women globally and is often accompanied by obesity and various levels of insulin resistance. Incretin-based therapies, including the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists liraglutide and semaglutide, and the dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) agonist tirzepatide, offer a biologically plausible mechanism for targeting metabolic dysfunction in PMOS. This review examines clinical trial evidence on the anthropometric and metabolic effects of incretin-based therapies in this population, including a focus on women of reproductive age, who face distinct challenges related to preconception planning, treatment duration, and post-discontinuation metabolic and weight management. Available literature shows that liraglutide, semaglutide and tirzepatide produce clinically meaningful reductions in body weight, body mass index (BMI), and waist circumference, with some studies also confirming preferential effects on visceral and ectopic fat compartments. Glycaemic and insulin resistance outcomes vary across studies, while lipid and blood pressure effects remain incompletely characterized. Although emerging data suggest that higher-potency agents may yield more consistent weight-loss benefits, available PMOS-specific evidence does not establish comparative metabolic superiority among agents. Interpretation of the available evidence is limited by the predominance of short-term trials at sub-obesity doses, frequent co-administration with metformin, and the absence of phenotype-stratified data, leaving the full metabolic potential of these agents in PMOS incompletely defined. Larger, longer, and higher-dose trials are needed to fully characterize the anthropometric and metabolic potential of these agents in PMOS.

title: SGLT-2 Inhibitors Versus GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Propensity Score-Matched Cohort Study Comparing Adherence and Persistence with Specific Reference to Cardiovascular Disease.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Poor adherence and persistence to sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2is) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are a critical issue in the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), especially in patients with cardiovascular disease (CVD). We aimed to compare adherence and persistence to these drugs in routine care. Methods: A retrospective propensity score-matched (PSM) cohort study was conducted using pharmacy claims data. Patients aged 40 years or older with T2DM initiating SGLT-2is or GLP-1 RAs from 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2024 were included. Adherence was measured using the Medication Possession Ratio (MPR), and persistence was defined as the time to discontinuation (gap ≥ 60 days between refills). Results: At the 1-year follow-up, the SGLT-2i cohort showed significantly higher adherence compared to the GLP-1 RA cohort (86.66% vs. 76.53%; OR = 2.02) and higher persistence (71.48% vs. 66.52% at 12 months; HR = 0.83). The main factors associated with lack of persistency were newly diagnosed T2DM (HR = 1.25) and insulin use (HR = 1.32). In the CVD subgroup, the differences in favor of the SGLT-2i cohort were more pronounced for adherence (89.57% vs. 78.12%; OR = 2.44) and persistence (73.9% vs. 63.59%; HR = 0.66). Conclusions: In real-world clinical practice, adherence and persistence rates were higher in patients on SGLT-2is compared to those on GLP-1 RAs, particularly in the CVD subgroup. Our findings suggest that the new strategies are necessary to improve adherence and persistence to these medications, particularly in patients with CVD.

title: Emerging Therapeutic Strategies for Child and Adolescent Obesity: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Childhood obesity is a chronic, multifactorial disease requiring attention to biological, behavioral, psychological, family, and socioeconomic factors. This narrative review examined the integration of lifestyle, family-based, psychological, and pharmacological approaches, focusing on treatment engagement, eating disorders, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and treatment durability. A single search interface covering PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science (the University of Turin library discovery platform) was used to identify studies published primarily from 2010 to August 2026. Pediatric trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, guidelines, and public-health reports were prioritized. Intensive family-based, multicomponent behavioral treatment remains the best-supported foundation of care, although psychological outcomes are infrequently assessed. Psychiatric comorbidity is heterogeneous; loss-of-control eating, emotional symptoms, ADHD, and executive-function difficulties may impair engagement in selected patients, and untreated ADHD has been associated with a slower BMI response to weight management. Professionally supervised obesity treatment containing a dietary component did not, on average, worsen eating psychopathology and reduced several related symptoms. Family participation improved outcomes, whereas logistical, socioeconomic, and psychological barriers reduced attendance. Across randomized trials, adding anti-obesity medication to behavioral treatment produced an additional, although on average modest, reduction in BMI. Semaglutide, liraglutide, and phentermine/topiramate produced larger numerical reductions than older agents in separate trials, but heterogeneity and the absence of head-to-head comparisons preclude formal ranking. Gastrointestinal adverse events were frequent with glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists. Pediatric trials and real-world evidence indicate partial weight regain after discontinuation, while prescribing remains limited and unequal. Pediatric obesity care should be phenotype-informed, multidisciplinary, and longitudinal. Pharmacotherapy can enhance BMI reduction but should complement rather than replace behavioral, psychological, and family care. Outcomes should extend beyond BMI to metabolic, psychological, functional, and long-term measures.

title: Retatrutide as a Unimolecular GIP/GLP-1/Glucagon Receptor Tri-Agonist: Molecular Design, Pharmaceutical Development and Critical Interpretation of Emerging Phase 3 Evidence.
abstract: Retatrutide (LY3437943) is an investigational, once-weekly, lipidated 39-residue peptide that activates the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide-1, and glucagon receptors. Its molecular design combines incretin activity with glucagon receptor engagement while maintaining glycaemic efficacy. This critical narrative review examines molecular engineering, pharmacokinetics, dose escalation, pharmaceutical development, and clinical evidence available through 11 September 2026. Five phase 3 trials have reported positive primary outcomes, but only TRANSCEND-T2D-1 has a full peer-reviewed report; the obesity trials are currently available as sponsor topline disclosures. In those disclosures, efficacy-estimand mean weight reductions of 28.3% at 80 weeks (TRIUMPH-1) and 28.7% at 68 weeks (TRIUMPH-4) were reported, with a TRIUMPH-1 treatment-regimen estimate of 25.0%; these values remain provisional pending full published trial reports. The peer-reviewed TRANSCEND-T2D-1 report supports glycaemic efficacy in early type 2 diabetes. Interpretation requires attention to estimands, population differences, treatment discontinuation and selection into trial extensions. Gastrointestinal adverse events, dysaesthesia, heart-rate changes and the functional consequences of lean-mass loss require further evaluation. Pharmaceutical priorities include scalable synthesis, impurity and potency control, formulation stability, immunogenicity and reliable dose delivery. Retatrutide provides a clinically advanced example of unimolecular poly-agonism, but comparative effectiveness, long-term outcomes and regulatory review remain essential to defining its therapeutic role.

title: Obesity and Atrial Fibrillation: Weighing the Evidence.
abstract: Obesity is a major, modifiable risk factor for atrial fibrillation (AF). Potential mechanisms include haemodynamic and metabolic changes, inflammation, changes in epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) composition and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome. EAT is increasingly recognised as a dynamic, pro-arrhythmic fat depot with a possible bidirectional relationship with AF, whereby AF itself may modulate EAT independent of weight change. CKM syndrome also underlies the complex interplay between obesity and AF. Despite guideline recommendations for at least 10% weight reduction in obese patients with AF, recent randomised trials focusing on weight reduction have largely failed to demonstrate clinically meaningful improvements in AF outcomes compared with catheter ablation or usual care. Incretin-based therapies including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are a promising therapy offering sustained weight loss alongside broader cardiometabolic benefits, although randomised trials with AF as a primary endpoint are lacking. Comprehensive multidisciplinary lifestyle risk factor modification (LRFM) clinics that address cardiometabolic risk factors, AF education and medication adherence have shown benefit beyond weight reduction alone, although their delivery has been heterogeneous. This narrative review examines the evolving relationship between obesity and AF including a multidimensional cardiometabolic lens, EAT characterisation, contemporary randomised trials of weight reduction, and the emerging role of incretin-based therapies and LRFM clinics.

title: Semaglutide in Patients with Obesity and Psoriasis: Insights from an 18-Month Real-World Experience.
abstract: Psoriasis is often associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) due to a common low-grade chronic inflammatory mechanism amplified by metabolic dysfunction. Biologics have revolutionized psoriasis treatment, but patients with obesity show reduced responses and higher discontinuation rates. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists-such as semaglutide-may enhance the efficacy of psoriasis care; however, data are limited in this context. We presented a retrospective analysis of our single-center real-world experience with 33 obese patients (24 men and 9 women) affected by mild (n = 19, 57.6%) or moderate (n = 14, 42.4%) psoriasis and treated with semaglutide over 18 months. Adherence to the semaglutide prescription was 94% (range 88-99%), with most patients (54.5%) having a last recorded dose of 1.0 mg. A significant mean reduction of 4.25 points in the PASI score (from 9.31 ± 1.54 to 5.05 ± 0.88; p < 0.001) was reported, followed by a mean decrease of 4.15 kg/m2 in BMI (from 32.53 ± 1.92 to 28.38 ± 1.59 kg/m2; p < 0.001) and significant improvements in all metabolic parameters. In addition, there was a significant decrease in inflammatory markers (CRP decreased from 5.47 ± 1.69 to 2.69 ± 0.94 mg/L, and ESR from 17.76 ± 4.22 to 11.64 ± 2.83 mm/h). More than fifty-seven percent (57.6%) of patients experienced mild and transitory gastrointestinal reactions, but no cases of discontinuation or cutaneous reaction occurred. Data provide additional insights into the role of semaglutide in patients with mild-to-moderate psoriasis. Large-scale, multicenter studies are needed to validate long-term results.

title: Real-World Effectiveness, Documented Adverse Events, and Treatment Adherence of Semaglutide and Liraglutide in Omani Patients: A Retrospective Observational Study.
abstract: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are widely used in obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), but comparative real-world evidence from the Middle East remains limited. We compared the effectiveness, documented adverse events, adherence and persistence of once-weekly semaglutide and once-daily liraglutide in Omani adults. Methods: Retrospective cohort study of adults treated with semaglutide or liraglutide at Sultan Qaboos University Hospital between January 2024 and December 2025. The primary outcome was change in body mass index (BMI) at 3 and 6 months; change in body weight, percentage total body weight loss and the proportions achieving at least 5% and at least 10% weight loss. Because treatment indication and exposure differed markedly between groups, the primary comparison used propensity-score overlap weighting with additional covariate adjustment, implemented in a design-based general linear model. A mixed model for repeated measures supported the primary analysis and handled missing visits under a missing-at-random assumption, with a delta-adjusted pattern-mixture analysis used to test departures from that assumption. Persistence was analysed with Kaplan-Meier estimation and Cox regression adjusted for baseline covariates only. Secondary outcomes were corrected for multiplicity using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Analyses are labelled throughout as primary, prespecified secondary, or post hoc exploratory. No patient received semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly, the dose licenced for chronic weight management, due to unavailability during the study period. Results: Of 287 treatment records supplied, 257 unique patients were analysed (liraglutide n = 135; semaglutide n = 122). Semaglutide was associated with a greater reduction in BMI than liraglutide at 3 months (adjusted difference -0.60 kg/m2, 95% CI -1.12 to -0.07; p = 0.026) and at 6 months (-1.42 kg/m2, 95% CI -2.60 to -0.24; p = 0.019). In clinical units, the adjusted difference in body weight was -1.70 kg at 3 months (95% CI -3.10 to -0.29; p = 0.018) and -3.66 kg at 6 months (95% CI -6.72 to -0.60; p = 0.020). At 6 months, 56.5% of semaglutide-treated and 24.7% of liraglutide-treated patients had lost at least 5% of body weight (p < 0.001), and 30.4% versus 4.9% had lost at least 10% (p < 0.001). The mixed model gave the same conclusion (group-by-time interaction p < 0.001). No statistically detectable difference in glycated hemoglobin HbA1c change was observed at either time point (p = 0.132 and p = 0.158; interaction p = 0.360). Of eight secondary cardiometabolic outcomes, only total cholesterol at 3 months remained significant after correction for multiplicity (adjusted p = 0.024). Documented adverse events were infrequent and did not differ between groups (12.6% versus 8.2%, p = 0.251). Hypoglycaemia occurred in seven liraglutide-treated and one semaglutide-treated patient (p = 0.069 by exact test) and was not significant after weighting and adjustment for background insulin or sulfonylurea use (p = 0.345). Crude discontinuation was 48.9% with liraglutide versus 9.0% with semaglutide, but median exposure was 17 versus 6 months. After accounting for time at risk, no difference in persistence was statistically apparent (log-rank p = 0.328; adjusted hazard ratio for semaglutide 1.60, 95% CI 0.61 to 4.19). Documented adherence was higher with semaglutide (95.9% versus 83.7%, p = 0.001). Conclusions: In this cohort, semaglutide was associated with a modestly greater reduction in BMI and body weight than liraglutide, and with a higher proportion of patients achieving clinically meaningful weight loss. Glycaemic and most cardiometabolic comparisons were inconclusive once confounding, multiplicity and limited precision were accounted for, and the large apparent difference in discontinuation was no longer statistically apparent after allowing for unequal time at risk. These findings are associative. They describe the drugs as prescribed in one health-care setting, at doses that are not pharmacologically equivalent, and should not be read as evidence of comparative causal superiority.

title: Weight Regain After Discontinuation of GLP-1 and GIP/GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Weight regain and loss of cardiometabolic benefit commonly follow the withdrawal of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/GLP-1 receptor agonists, yet maintenance strategies are incompletely characterized. We conducted a systematic review reported according to PRISMA 2020 of primary studies in adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes. PubMed/MEDLINE, Europe PMC and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to September 2026, supplemented by backward/forward citation searching and cross-checking of recent systematic reviews. Eligible reports quantified weight or cardiometabolic outcomes at least 12 weeks after planned or unplanned treatment cessation, or tested a post-cessation maintenance strategy. Randomized reports were assessed with RoB 2 and non-randomized reports with ROBINS-I. Owing to incompatible estimands, follow-up schedules, cointerventions and overlapping trial families, results were synthesized narratively without a new pooled estimate. Eighteen reports representing 16 study families were included. Randomized withdrawal trials showed renewed weight gain after treatment cessation: +6.9% over 48 weeks after switching from semaglutide to placebo in STEP 4, and +14.0% over 52 weeks after switching from tirzepatide to placebo in SURMOUNT-4. In the STEP 1 extension, participants regained 11.6 percentage points over one year, approximately two-thirds of their prior loss, while several cardiometabolic measures moved toward baseline. Real-world estimates were smaller and more variable because discontinuation was often inferred from prescriptions, follow-up weights were missing, and many patients restarted or switched therapy. Cardiometabolic rebound was associated with the degree of weight regain, but clinical cardiovascular events were not evaluated. Evidence for maintenance strategies was sparse: one randomized post-treatment study supported supervised exercise, with the exercise-plus-liraglutide group retaining an additional 5.1 kg of weight loss one year after both interventions ended compared with liraglutide alone; a small pilot supported sitagliptin plus metformin after liraglutide in polycystic ovary syndrome. No eligible controlled trial isolated a specific diet after cessation. Weight regain is frequent after stopping GLP-1-based therapy, although magnitude varies by drug, design, follow-up and subsequent treatment. Structured exercise may help reduce regain and preserve lean mass, but evidence for dietary, behavioral, tapering or pharmacologic transition strategies remains limited. Discontinuation should therefore be planned as part of chronic obesity care, with explicit monitoring and shared decision-making, rather than presented as a predictable short course.

title: Oral Health-Related Adverse Events of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.
abstract: As the clinical use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) continues to grow for the management of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular and renal protection, noncirrhotic fatty liver disease, and weight management, their potential implications for oral health need to be considered. This study examined oral health-related adverse events (AEs) associated with GLP-1 RAs using postmarketing data from the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). FAERS reports for available GLP-1 RAs, exenatide, liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide, and tirzepatide, were screened from their initial market introduction through December 2025, identifying 364,274 total AE reports, of which 31,195 (8.6%) involved oral, craniofacial, or dental manifestations. Tirzepatide, despite being one of the most recently approved GLP-1 RAs, accounted for the highest overall AE volume, and semaglutide demonstrated the largest proportion of oral health-related AEs. A disproportionality analysis revealed a significant drug-specific signal for dry mouth of semaglutide, while vomiting, regurgitation, and reflux-related events produced a significant signal across all 5 drugs. Sensory disorders, including dysgeusia and taste disturbances, also demonstrated significant proportional reporting ratios (PRRs) and reporting odds ratios (RORs) for several GLP-1 RAs. Association analysis of AEs showed significant associations between vomiting and taste disturbances, as well as between dry mouth and dysgeusia, particularly with semaglutide and dulaglutide. This analysis highlights emerging safety signals in oral health and underscores the need for heightened clinical awareness and prospective studies to characterize the incidence, timing, and mechanisms of oral AEs associated with GLP-1 RA therapy.Knowledge Transfer Statement:Understanding the oral adverse effects associated with GLP-1 receptor agonists allows clinicians and dental providers to more effectively counsel patients initiating or continuing these medications. By recognizing early symptoms such as dry mouth, dysgeusia, and reflux-related irritation, providers can implement targeted preventive strategies-including hydration guidance, salivary substitutes, dietary modifications, and closer oral health monitoring-to reduce complications and improve patient comfort, adherence, and overall treatment outcomes. This knowledge enhances interdisciplinary management of individuals using GLP-1 RAs.

title: Efficacy and Safety of CagriSema in Type 2 Diabetes: A Dose- and Comparator-Specific Systematic Review and Bayesian Meta-Analysis.
abstract: CagriSema combines cagrilintide with semaglutide and may improve glycaemic control and body weight in Type 2 diabetes. We evaluated its dose- and comparator-specific efficacy and safety. PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched through 30 June 2026 for randomized controlled trials. Analyses were stratified by CagriSema dose and comparator. For HbA1c and body weight, efficacy/trial-product estimands were aligned where sufficiently reported, with treatment-policy estimates examined in sensitivity analyses. Bayesian random-effects models generated posterior medians and 95% credible intervals (CrIs). Six trials representing 4554 potentially eligible participants with Type 2 diabetes were included. Compared with placebo, CagriSema 2.4 mg produced between-group differences of -1.87 percentage points in HbA1c (95% CrI, -2.08 to -1.62) and -12.69 percentage points in percentage body-weight change (95% CrI, -13.78 to -11.61). Versus semaglutide 2.4 mg, the additional HbA1c reduction was modest and uncertain (-0.21 percentage points; 95% CrI, -0.62 to 0.11), whereas additional body-weight reduction remained probable (-5.84 percentage points; 95% CrI, -10.08 to -2.15). Gastrointestinal adverse events and adverse-event-related discontinuation were increased versus placebo (RR, 2.27 [95% CrI, 1.81 - 3.00] and 3.16 [1.50 to 6.87], respectively), while estimates versus semaglutide were less precise. CagriSema provides substantial glycaemic and body-weight benefits versus placebo. Its incremental advantage over dose-matched semaglutide is more evident for body-weight reduction, while comparative gastrointestinal tolerability and discontinuation risk remain uncertain.

title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist use and risk of postmastectomy lymphedema in breast cancer survivors: a multicenter real-world cohort study.
journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
abstract: Postmastectomy lymphedema is a chronic survivorship complication after breast cancer treatment, particularly among patients exposed to axillary surgery. Obesity and metabolic inflammation are recognized contributors to lymphedema risk. This study evaluated whether glucagon-like peptide - 1 receptor agonist exposure was associated with lower incidence of coded postmastectomy lymphedema among breast cancer patients with mastectomy and/or axillary procedure exposure. We performed a retrospective cohort study using deidentified electronic health record data from the TriNetX Research Network. Adult patients with breast cancer and coded mastectomy and/or axillary procedural exposure were stratified by GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure versus no exposure. One-to-one propensity score matching was used to balance measured baseline characteristics. The primary outcome was incident coded postmastectomy lymphedema syndrome. Outcomes were assessed from 1 to 650 days after the index event using risk estimates, Kaplan-Meier analysis, and Cox proportional hazards models. After propensity score matching, 61,630 patients were included, with 30,815 patients in each cohort. Coded postmastectomy lymphedema occurred in 258 of 29,259 GLP-1 receptor agonist users and 779 of 30,237 non-users, corresponding to incidence rates of 0.88% and 2.58%, respectively. GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure was associated with lower incidence of coded postmastectomy lymphedema in time-to-event analysis (hazard ratio 0.373, 95% CI 0.324-0.429; p < 0.001). The absolute risk difference was - 1.7%, with an estimated number needed to treat of 59. In this large real-world breast cancer surgical/procedural cohort, GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure was associated with lower incidence of coded postmastectomy lymphedema over 650 days of follow-up. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation with systematic lymphedema assessment and detailed characterization of GLP-1 receptor agonist timing, duration, dose, and adherence.

title: Glucagon-like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Heart Transplant Recipients With Type 2 Diabetes: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is frequent after heart transplantation (HT) and is exacerbated by immunosuppressive therapy. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) may improve metabolic control, but data in HT recipients are limited. We performed a retrospective, multicenter study including HT recipients with T2DM from 14 Spanish centers. In patients treated with GLP-1 RAs, we assessed antidiabetic and immunosuppressive therapies, adverse events, and changes in metabolic parameters, insulin dose, and immunosuppressant trough levels during the first year after GLP-1 RA initiation. Among 734 HT recipients with T2DM (2011-2021), 108 (14.7%) received GLP-1 RAs (mean age 55.4 ± 9.0 y; 79.6% male), initiated 4.0 ± 3.1 y post-HT. At baseline, 64.8% had obesity. Semaglutide was used in 59%, dulaglutide in 27%, liraglutide in 13%, and tirzepatide in 1%; 41.7% achieved the maximum therapeutic dose. After 1 y, significant reductions were observed in body weight (-6.2 kg; 95% confidence interval [CI], -7.7 to -4.5 kg), fasting glucose (-27 mg/dL; 95% CI, -41 to -7 mg/dL), glycated hemoglobin (-0.74%; 95% CI, -1.12% to -0.35%), total cholesterol (-12 mg/dL; 95% CI, -19 to -6 mg/dL), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (-8 mg/dL; 95% CI, -14 to -2 mg/dL), triglycerides (-29 mg/dL; 95% CI, -53 to -5 mg/dL), and systolic blood pressure (-3.6 mm Hg; 95% CI, -6.4 to -0.9 mm Hg). Tacrolimus trough levels decreased modestly (-0.7 ng/mL; 95% CI, -1.4 to -0.1 ng/mL; P = 0.025), without episodes of acute rejection. Gastrointestinal adverse events occurred in 12.0%, leading to discontinuation in 3.7%. In HT recipients with T2DM, GLP-1 RAs were associated with improved glycemic and cardiometabolic parameters and were generally well tolerated. These findings support the use of GLP-1 RAs as a valuable therapeutic strategy for the management of T2DM after HT.

title: Cutaneous Adverse Events Associated with Semaglutide, Liraglutide and Tirzepatide: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Incretin-based therapies, including glucagon like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 RAs, are increasingly prescribed for obesity, leading to greater recognition of associated dermatological adverse events (AEs). We aimed to characterize the spectrum, frequency, and clinical characteristics of cutaneous AEs reported with semaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide, focusing on these agents because of their established use in both weight management and diabetes mellitus. A systematic literature search was conducted in MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, and Web of Science. Search terms combined skin-related manifestations (e.g., skin, dermatologic, injection-site reactions, pruritus, rash, hypersensitivity, dysesthesia, vasculitis) with GLP-1 RA and GIP/GLP-1 RAs (semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide). Clinical trials, observational studies, pharmacovigilance studies, and case reports reporting skin-related AEs associated with semaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide were included. One hundred and one studies were included (32 randomized controlled trials, 6 retrospective cohort/cross-sectional studies, 20 pharmacovigilance studies, and 43 case series/reports). Cutaneous AEs ranged from generally common but mild reactions to rare but potentially severe immune-mediated disorders. Injection-site reactions, including erythema, pruritus, and hemorrhage, were reported most frequently with tirzepatide (2-7%), then liraglutide, and less commonly with semaglutide, with evidence of dose dependence. Dysesthesia was most strongly associated with semaglutide, occurring in approximately 5% of patients at standard doses and up to 20% with high-dose formulations indicated for weight management, with events frequently occurring during dose escalation. Uncommon reactions reported in association with GLP-1 or GIP/GLP-1 RA use included angioedema, hypersensitivity reactions, autoimmune blistering diseases, drug eruptions, vasculitis, and severe cutaneous reactions. Although most cutaneous AEs associated with GLP-1 and GIP/GLP-1 RAs are mild and manageable, clinically relevant drug-specific differences exist. The recognition of common and uncommon skin manifestations may facilitate earlier diagnosis, support treatment adherence, and reduce the adverse outcomes.

title: Post-Initiation Care Patterns and Weight Loss With Semaglutide and Tirzepatide for Obesity in Clinical Practice.
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: Randomized trials show substantial weight loss with semaglutide and tirzepatide under structured care, but little is known about whether patients in routine practice continue therapy, reach a maintenance dose, and have their weight measured. To describe the first year after initiation of semaglutide or tirzepatide for obesity, including care patterns, maintenance-dose attainment, weight documentation, and total body weight loss (TBWL). This retrospective cohort study used Epic Cosmos, an electronic health record network of >350 US health systems, to identify adults with obesity and without diabetes who initiated injectable semaglutide or tirzepatide in 2024. Outcomes over 12 months included prescribing persistence, discontinuation, switching, add-on therapy, and reinitiation; attainment of Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-labeled maintenance doses; availability of follow-up weight; and TBWL across progressively restricted populations. Among 743,153 adults (60.1% semaglutide; mean age, 48.5 years; 72.5% female), 12-month prescribing persistence was 29.9% for semaglutide and 35.9% for tirzepatide. FDA-labeled maintenance-dose attainment was 28.3% and 55.0%, respectively, and only 8.8% and 16.4% remained prescribing persistent at a maintenance dose with a recorded weight at 12 months. About half of initiators lacked a 12-month weight. Among all initiators, ≥5% TBWL was documented in 25.6% (semaglutide) and 30.4% (tirzepatide), rising to 51.9% and 61.9% among those with recorded weight, 66.1% and 79.5% among those also prescribing persistent, and 82.9% and 87.3% among those further at a maintenance dose. In routine practice, most patients initiating semaglutide or tirzepatide did not remain on therapy, reach a maintenance dose, and have weight documented through the first year. Documented weight loss was greatest among those completing each step of care, suggesting continuation, dose escalation, and monitoring as targets for improvement. Care Cascade and Weight-Loss Outcomes Among Semaglutide and Tirzepatide Initiators, Standardized to 100 Initiators.Numbers are per 100 initiators and were rounded so that categories at each step sum to the preceding step. At the 12-month dose step, prescribed dose was missing for 1 per 100 semaglutide initiators and <1 per 100 tirzepatide initiators.

title: Parasympathetic dysfunction assessed by deep-breathing CVR-R is associated with early discontinuation of oral semaglutide in type 2 diabetes: A multicenter retrospective study.
abstract: Although glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists are widely used for type 2 diabetes, gastrointestinal intolerance frequently leads to early discontinuation. Predictors of oral semaglutide discontinuation remain poorly defined, and its formulation-specific dependence on gastric conditions may influence tolerability. We examined whether the coefficient of variation of R-R intervals (CVR-R) was associated with discontinuation within 6 months. In this multicenter retrospective study, 203 consecutive patients initiating oral semaglutide between February 2021 and December 2024 were screened, and 61 were analyzed after exclusions. The Discontinuation Group (n = 21) discontinued because of nausea and/or vomiting within 6 months, whereas the Maintenance Group (n = 40) continued for ≥ 6 months. CVR-R was assessed at rest (CVR-R_rest) and during deep breathing (CVR-R_DB). Associations with discontinuation were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression; exploratory machine learning and time-to-event analyses were performed. CVR-R_DB was lower in the Discontinuation Group than in the Maintenance Group (median 1.93% vs 3.26%, P < 0.001). CVR-R_DB remained independently associated with discontinuation after adjustment for age and sex (adjusted OR 0.191; 95% CI 0.071-0.512; P = 0.001; AUC 0.832) and further adjustment for neuropathy stage. The AUC was numerically higher for the age- and sex-adjusted model containing CVR-R_DB than for that containing CVR-R_rest (0.832 vs 0.699; DeLong P = 0.085). An internally derived CVR-R_DB cutoff of 2.55% stratified 6-month persistence (43.3% vs 87.1%; log-rank P < 0.001), and machine learning analyses prioritized CVR-R_DB. Lower CVR-R during deep breathing was associated with early oral semaglutide discontinuation due to nausea and/or vomiting. CVR-R_DB may support risk stratification at initiation.

title: Durability of Semaglutide Effects After Treatment Discontinuation in HIV-Associated Lipohypertrophy: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Phase 2b Clinical Trial.
abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-associated lipohypertrophy is characterized by excess central and visceral adiposity and is associated with increased cardiometabolic risk among people with HIV (PWH). In a previously reported randomized trial, semaglutide significantly reduced body weight, regional adiposity, and insulin resistance over 32 weeks of active treatment. However, the durability of these benefits after treatment discontinuation is unknown. We conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in PWH with HIV-associated lipohypertrophy. Participants were randomized to semaglutide or placebo for 32 weeks, followed by discontinuation of study drug and observational follow-up through week 56. The current analysis investigated effects of semaglutide at week 56, as compared to baseline and week 32. Outcomes included adipose tissue quantity by body compartment. Analyses were performed using intention-to-treat principles. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04019197) and is complete. Of 108 participants initially randomized, 92 completed the 32-week intervention and 80 participants (39 semaglutide, 41 placebo) completed the posttreatment phase. Participants previously assigned to semaglutide experienced increases in body weight, body mass index (BMI), waist circumference, total body fat, and visceral adipose tissue between weeks 32 and 56, accompanied by worsening glycemic indices and insulin resistance. Despite this rebound, net reductions in body weight, BMI, and waist circumference were retained at week 56 compared with baseline. Placebo-treated participants demonstrated relative stability across outcomes. Discontinuation of semaglutide in PWH with lipohypertrophy resulted in partial loss of improvements in weight, adiposity, and metabolic parameters. These findings support that sustained pharmacologic exposure is likely needed to achieve long-term benefit.

title: Efficacy and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists for antipsychotic-related overweight and metabolic dysregulation: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Antipsychotic-related overweight and metabolic dysregulation are highly prevalent among patients with severe mental illness. Although glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated substantial metabolic benefits in the general population, their efficacy and safety in antipsychotic-treated patients remain unclear. This review aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of GLP-1RAs in patients with antipsychotic-related overweight and metabolic dysregulation. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating GLP-1RAs in adults receiving antipsychotic treatment. PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to September 13, 2026. Primary outcomes included changes in body weight, body mass index (BMI), HbA1c, and total cholesterol. Random-effects models were used to pool mean differences (MDs) and risk ratios (RRs). This study was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261290294). Eight RCTs involving 535 randomized participants were included. GLP-1RAs treatment was associated with significant reductions in body weight (MD = -6.54 kg, 95% CI: -9.80 to -3.29, P < 0.001, I2 = 92%), BMI (MD = -2.34 kg/m2, 95% CI: -3.34 to -1.34, P < 0.001, I² = 85%), HbA1c (MD = -0.32%, 95% CI: -0.39 to -0.26, P < 0.001, I² = 52%), waist circumference (MD = -5.22 cm, 95% CI: -6.55 to -3.88, P < 0.001, I2 = 27%), visceral fat mass (MD = -0.31 kg, 95% CI: -0.46 to -0.16, P < 0.001, I2 = 11%), and LDL-C (MD = -0.16 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.31 to -0.01, P = 0.03, I2 = 54%), whereas no significant effects were observed for total cholesterol, triglycerides, or HDL-C. Weight reduction was greatest with semaglutide, followed by liraglutide, and increased with longer treatment duration (both P for subgroup differences < 0.05). GLP-1RAs were associated with higher risks of nausea (RR = 1.61, 95% CI: 1.20 to 2.16), vomiting (RR = 2.10, 95% CI: 1.32 to 3.35), and constipation (RR = 2.34, 95% CI: 1.23 to 4.47), but not of diarrhea, serious adverse events (RR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.49 to 1.06), all-cause discontinuation (RR = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.60 to 1.85), or discontinuation due to adverse events (RR = 2.14, 95% CI: 0.72 to 6.33). Psychiatric adverse events were infrequent and could not be pooled. GLP-1RAs significantly improve weight-related and glycemic outcomes in antipsychotic-treated patients, at the cost of an increased risk of gastrointestinal adverse events. Their psychiatric safety could not be established owing to sparse data. Longer-term trials with standardized safety reporting are warranted.

title: How Well Are We Measuring Nausea? A Narrative Review of Patient-Reported Outcome Gaps in GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Obesity Trials.
abstract: Across the full spectrum of major clinical trials evaluating glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) for obesity management, nausea consistently emerges as the most documented adverse effect, yet the methods used to capture it have received little scrutiny relative to their clinical importance. This narrative review traces how nausea was actually measured across the pivotal liraglutide (SCALE), semaglutide (STEP) and tirzepatide (SURMOUNT) obesity trial programmes, and situates those methods against the standards set out in the Consensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN) and the United States Food and Drug Administration's Patient-Focused Drug Development guidance. Across all three drug classes, nausea was ascertained through investigator-recorded, spontaneously reported adverse events coded to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), a pharmacovigilance framework built for a different purpose than symptom characterization, rather than through any validated, symptom-specific patient-reported outcome instrument. This observation gains further importance when considered alongside a second, less widely recognized fact: these same trial programmes devoted substantial methodological effort to developing and implementing a rigorous, quality of life measure specifically for obesity, the Impact of Weight on Quality of Life-Lite Clinical Trials Version in addition to the Short Form-36 and EuroQol-5D. We argue that this asymmetry, more than any single mismeasurement, helps explain why real-world persistence with these agents falls so far short of what trial-reported tolerability figures would predict, and we outline what a fit-for-purpose metabolic nausea instrument would need to capture that adverse-event surveillance cannot.

title: New Horizons for Incretin-Based Therapeutics.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-based therapies marked a major breakthrough in obesity pharmacotherapy, while subsequent advancements targeting multiple entero-pancreatic hormones now deliver weight loss previously achievable only with bariatric surgery, alongside improvements in obesity-related complications. Despite this progress, significant challenges persist, including reduced efficacy in diabetic populations, gastrointestinal adverse effects, and high costs that drive a real-world adherence gap. Consequently, next-generation therapies, including receptor polyagonists, oral formulations, and small-molecule incretin mimetics with optimized pharmacokinetic profiles, are being developed to enhance efficacy, tolerability, and accessibility while maintaining safety. However, weight regain after treatment cessation remains a critical hurdle. Growing evidence underscores the importance of sustained lifestyle interventions and muscle mass preservation to facilitate weight stabilization. Concurrently, research is heavily focused on identifying the biological drivers of weight regain, such as altered neuroregulation, metabolic adaptation, and adipose tissue remodeling. This review examines the current landscape, limitations, and emerging strategies of obesity pharmacotherapy.

title: Case Report: Panic attacks after tirzepatide injection in two female patients with recurrent depressive disorder.
journal: Frontiers in drug safety and regulation
abstract: Tirzepatide was introduced several years ago for the management of obesity. Its side-effect profile includes gastrointestinal symptoms and hormonal shifts similar to other glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs). This class of medications is currently being investigated for its potential utility in treating depressive and anxiety disorders. While safety data generally indicate a low risk for adverse psychiatric events - such as suicidal ideation or depressive episodes - and some evidence suggests a beneficial impact on mood, anecdotal reports have linked these agents to panic attacks. However, scientific evidence for this remains limited. We present the cases of two female patients with histories of depressive disorder who experienced panic attacks following tirzepatide injections for weight loss. Both required hospitalization for the exacerbation of moderate-to-severe recurrent depressive disorder. The panic attacks occurred in close temporal proximity to the injections and resolved upon discontinuation. No clear medical aetiology was identified. Changes in pharmacokinetics by delayed gastric emptying, GABAergic deficits, an activation of the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) or activation of the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis are considered as potential mechanisms for panic attacks.

title: 12-month weight-loss trajectories and predictors of response to tirzepatide under individualized dosing: A multicenter real-world study.
abstract: Real-world evidence on 12-month treatment effectiveness and persistence with tirzepatide remains limited, particularly under individualized dosing and self-funded treatment conditions. We evaluated 12-month tirzepatide outcomes in routine clinical practice. This was a multicenter, retrospective, observational real-world study including 249 adults with overweight or obesity treated with tirzepatide across 13 obesity practices in Greece. Treatment was entirely self-funded, and dose escalation was individualized rather than protocol driven. Treatment persistence, reasons for discontinuation, weight loss, dose trajectories, metabolic outcomes, and predictors of 12-month response were evaluated. At 12 months, 170/249 patients (68.3%) remained on treatment, 64 (25.7%) had confirmed discontinuation, and 15 (6.0%) were lost to follow-up. Among patients with available weight measurements, mean weight loss was 19.9 ± 8.6% at 12 months, with 88.9%, 50.0%, and 27.2% achieving ≥10%, ≥20%, and ≥25% weight loss, respectively. Mean tirzepatide dose at 12 months was 9.71 mg. Among 179 patients assessed at both 6 and 12 months, 70.4% experienced >2% additional weight loss during the second 6 months, whereas 10.1% experienced >2% weight regain. Six-month percentage weight loss was not significantly associated with additional weight loss between months 6 and 12 after multivariable adjustment (β = -0.110, P = 0.135).
