Among 139 participants who had not achieved ≥20% weight loss at month 6, early response demonstrated moderate discrimination for achieving this cumulative threshold at month 12 (AUC 0.760, 95% bootstrap CI 0.675-0.837), with an adjusted OR of 1.34 per additional percentage point of 6-month weight loss (P < 0.001). In a fully self-funded real-world setting, tirzepatide was associated with substantial weight loss and high documented treatment persistence over 12 months. Six-month weight-loss response was associated with the likelihood of achieving ≥20% weight loss at 12 months. These findings do not establish long-term weight maintenance beyond the observation period.

title: Safety outcomes of semaglutide by chronic kidney disease severity in the FLOW trial.
abstract: People with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) often experience medication intolerance and side effects that worsen with lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). This prespecified secondary analysis assessed the safety of semaglutide by baseline eGFR. FLOW (NCT03819153) was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial testing the efficacy of subcutaneous semaglutide 1.0 mg once-weekly on a primary kidney outcome (50% or more eGFR reduction, kidney failure, or death due to kidney or cardiovascular causes) in participants with T2D and CKD. Safety data were collected selectively and included serious adverse events (SAEs), AEs leading to treatment discontinuation, and prespecified AEs of special interest (AESIs). In this descriptive assessment, systematically collected safety data were reported numerically by baseline eGFR. Of 3533 participants, 1767 received semaglutide and 1766 received placebo. Fewer SAEs were reported with semaglutide than placebo across baseline eGFR subgroups (45.1% versus 50.4% in the 60 or more ml/min per 1.73 m2 subgroup, and 56.4% versus 60.4% in the under 30 ml/min per 1.73 m2 subgroup). SAEs related to infections and infestations; cardiac disorders; respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorders; and metabolism and nutrition disorders were generally less frequent with semaglutide than placebo, regardless of baseline eGFR. Treatment discontinuations due to AEs were higher with lower baseline eGFR across treatment groups (60 or more ml/min per 1.73 m2: semaglutide 11.2%, placebo 11.3%; under30 ml/min per 66 1.73 m2: semaglutide 18.8%, placebo 18.7%). Discontinuations specifically due to gastrointestinal AEs were reported more frequently with semaglutide (4.5%) than placebo (1.1%), regardless of baseline eGFR. Frequencies of AESI were similar between treatment groups across baseline eGFR subgroups. In this safety assessment, SAEs were reported less frequently with semaglutide than placebo, with corresponding patterns observed for treatment discontinuations and AESIs. No unexpected safety concerns were identified across the spectrum of eGFR represented in the FLOW trial.

title: Dose-response profiles in incretin and multi-agonist obesity pharmacotherapy.
journal: Clinics and research in hepatology and gastroenterology
abstract: Incretin and multi-agonist therapies have transformed obesity pharmacotherapy, but dose selection remains less mature than efficacy assessment. This critical narrative review examines nonlinear relationships among administered dose, systemic exposure, weight and cardiometabolic benefit, gastrointestinal tolerability, treatment persistence, and maintenance. Across established and newer programs, average efficacy generally increases with dose, yet incremental gains may narrow at higher exposure while adverse-event burden and discontinuation can increase. The maturity of evidence is heterogeneous, and later-stage programs should not be interpreted as clinically equivalent to agents supported mainly by earlier-phase dose-ranging data. Moreover, an "optimal dose" is not an endpoint-independent quantity: the exposure most appropriate for weight loss may differ from that relevant to glycemic control, cardiovascular benefit, body composition, tolerability, or maintenance. We therefore distinguish nominal dose from exposure and present response-guided titration as a hypothesis-generating framework for prospective testing, not as an evidence-based dosing algorithm. Existing continuation and withdrawal studies support the importance of ongoing pharmacological treatment after successful weight loss but do not establish a minimum or optimal de-intensified maintenance dose. Future trials should jointly model efficacy, safety, body composition, patient-reported outcomes, pharmacokinetics, and discontinuation to test objective-specific, patient-level dosing strategies.

title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and aesthetic surgery: perioperative safety, timing, durability and body composition.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and dual incretin agonists have transformed the management of obesity and type 2 diabetes and are rapidly reshaping the population seeking aesthetic surgery. By producing double-digit percentage weight loss, these agents expand eligibility for elective procedures while generating new patterns of skin redundancy, soft-tissue laxity, and facial volume depletion that drive demand for body contouring and facial rejuvenation. At the same time, incretin therapy introduces distinct perioperative considerations: delayed gastric emptying with possible pulmonary aspiration in symptomatic patients, gastrointestinal adverse effects that peak during dose escalation, loss of lean mass with rapid weight reduction, nutritional inadequacy during profound appetite suppression, and frequent weight regain after drug discontinuation, which threatens the durability of surgical results. This mini-review synthesizes current evidence on the mechanisms of GLP-1 RAs relevant to the reconstructive surgical patient, summarizes the evolving guidance from anesthesia societies, moving from blanket preoperative withholding to individualized risk stratification, reviews emerging outcome data on body contouring in GLP-1 RA users, and discusses body composition, sarcopenia risk, and nutritional optimization. We propose a pragmatic framework, anchored in weight stability and symptom burden, for timing elective aesthetic procedures relative to GLP-1 RA initiation, escalation, and maintenance, along with a multidisciplinary perioperative algorithm that links the endocrinologist, plastic surgeon, and anesthesiologist. As incretin-based pharmacotherapy expands globally, coordinated endocrine-surgical-anesthetic care will be essential to maximize safety, functional recovery, and patient satisfaction in the GLP-1 era.

title: Real-World Semaglutide Initiation Behaviours in the United States: Impact on Early Treatment Discontinuation and on 1-Year Persistence.
abstract: Little is known about how glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) are initiated in real-world settings and whether prescribing behaviours in routine care contribute to the high discontinuation rates seen in practice. We examined prescribing behaviours for injectable semaglutide at treatment initiation and evaluated their impact on early medication discontinuation and on 1-year persistence among US adults. Using MarketScan data (2018-2021), this retrospective cohort study identified US adults with diabetes and/or obesity on no prior incretin therapy starting injectable semaglutide. Initiating dose was categorized as low or high (≤ 0.5 and ≥ 1.0 mg/week, respectively); treatment status was followed for 12 months. Medication persistence was estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Piecewise Cox proportional hazards regression assessed early discontinuation risk, logistic regression assessed the odds of high-dose initiation. Among this cohort of 48 658 adults, 14.5% were started on semaglutide using high doses. The off-label high-dose regimen was associated with decreased 1-year persistence (p = 0.01), and a 25% increase in early discontinuation risk (HR: 1.25, 95% CI: 1.17-1.34, p < 0.001) independently of age, obesity status, co-morbidity measures and cost. Odds of high-dose initiation were increased in the West and South (p < 0.001), for endocrinologists (p = 0.02), for patients who were male (p < 0.001), younger (p = 0.02), with obesity versus overweight (p = 0.002), and for treatment initiation in 2018 compared with 2019-2021 (p < 0.001). Initiation of injectable semaglutide therapy using high doses is common in real-world settings. High-dose initiation represents a modifiable risk factor for early medication discontinuation and decreased 1-year persistence.

title: Patient-Reported Outcomes Following Initiation or Simplification of Treatment With iGlarLixi in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Given the significant burden that diabetes self-management poses, it is important to assess patient-reported outcomes (PROs) for Type 2 diabetes (T2D) treatments in clinical trials and real-world studies. Complex insulin regimens are associated with increased risk of hypoglycaemia and body weight gain, which could negatively impact treatment adherence and, therefore, achievement of glycaemic targets. iGlarLixi is a once-daily fixed-ratio combination of insulin glargine 100 U/mL and the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), lixisenatide. iGlarLixi is an effective treatment alternative to complex insulin regimens, with a favourable between-group difference in body weight and reduced risk of hypoglycaemia. This is the first review to summarise data from multiple validated PRO measures for recent iGlarLixi studies (Soli-CGM, SoliMix, Soli-SWITCH, IDEAL, SUCCESS and SIMPLIFY JP), including: Global Treatment Effectiveness Evaluation, Audit of Diabetes Dependent Quality of Life, Diabetes Medication Satisfaction Tool, Diabetes Therapy-Related Quality of Life, Diabetes Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire, Hypoglycaemic Attitudes and Behaviour Scale and Treatment-Related Impact Measure Diabetes. In clinical studies, once-daily iGlarLixi was associated with numerical improvements in selected treatment satisfaction measures in those who switched from: complex insulin regimens (once- or twice-daily premixed insulin and basal-bolus insulin), basal insulin or oral glucose-lowering medications. Additionally, in real-world studies, iGlarLixi was generally associated with improvements in treatment satisfaction and quality of life outcomes in adults with T2D who previously received basal-bolus insulin or oral glucose-lowering medications ± basal insulin or GLP-1 RAs. In conclusion, a once-daily injection of iGlarLixi may offer a clinically beneficial, simplified treatment option for adults with T2D compared with complex insulin-based regimens.

title: Weight Regain After Incretin Treatment: The Lean Mass Deficit Hypothesis and a Role for Testosterone Combination Therapy in Men.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1RA and triple (GIP)/GLP-1RA/glucagon agonists achieve placebo-subtracted weight loss of 15% to 22%. Their long-term value depends on how well the weight loss is maintained and on the composition of weight loss, not only amount of weight loss. Part of incretin-induced weight loss is lean tissue. It is unknown whether the proportion of lean mass, and especially, muscle mass loss is greater than with other weight-loss interventions, and whether it may cause clinically meaningful harm. Men with obesity commonly have low or low-normal testosterone, which is associated with reduced muscle mass, increased visceral adiposity, impaired insulin sensitivity, and increased cardiovascular risk. We propose, as an exploratory hypothesis, that in men with obesity and low testosterone, combining incretin therapy with testosterone therapy may preserve muscle mass, increase the proportion of weight lost as fat mass, and reduce fat-predominant weight regain after incretin discontinuation. Resistance exercise and adequate protein intake are first-line measures for preserving muscle mass during weight loss. No lifestyle measure reliably prevents the fat-predominant weight regain that follows diet discontinuation, and long-term adherence to lifestyle interventions is poor. We position testosterone therapy as a pharmacological adjunct for weight loss maintenance in men with obesity and low testosterone, to be evaluated in clinical trials. The only direct human data come from a small, non-randomized pilot study and are hypothesis-generating. The clinical consequences of incretin-associated loss of lean mass, and particularly muscle mass, should be investigated in future studies. The hypothesis requires evaluation in randomized controlled trials that properly assess changes in lean mass and muscle mass, along with safety monitoring, before it can inform clinical practice.

title: Economic evaluation of tirzepatide, semaglutide, and liraglutide in the treatment of obese and overweight patients without diabetes: a short-term cost-effectiveness analysis in Iran.
journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
abstract: GLP-1 and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists have improved obesity treatment, but their high cost requires economic evaluation to guide resource allocation. To assess the short-term cost-effectiveness of subcutaneous tirzepatide, semaglutide, and liraglutide for treating adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes in Iran. A decision-tree model was developed to compare tirzepatide, semaglutide, and liraglutide over 68 weeks in adults aged ≥ 18 years with BMI ≥ 30 kg/m² or ≥ 27 kg/m² with at least one additional weight-related complication, excluding those with diabetes, from the payer perspective. Clinical effectiveness, adverse event (AE), and treatment discontinuation data were obtained from published literatures. Quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) were estimated based on BMI changes and AE-related disutility. Direct medical costs included drug acquisition and AE management costs. Deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were performed. Compared with semaglutide, tirzepatide generated greater health benefits but at higher costs, resulting in an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of US$34,423.89/QALY. Liraglutide was dominated by semaglutide. Semaglutide was cost-effective at the Iranian willingness-to-pay threshold of US$ (Purchasing power parity (PPP) 15,558.5/QALY, equal to one time GDP per capita in 2026. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings. Semaglutide was the cost-effective injectable GLP-1-based therapy in Iran. Although tirzepatide provided greater health benefits, its higher cost limited its cost-effectiveness at current prices. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40200-026-02114-z.

title: Adherence and Persistence to Injectable versus Oral GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Comparative Systematic Review and Analysis.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) requires sustained glycemic control to prevent long-term complications. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are effective therapies, traditionally administered via injection. The introduction of oral formulations, such as oral semaglutide, may improve patient adherence and persistence. A systematic review with descriptive pooled synthesis was conducted using studies identified from PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and relevant real-world observational data sources. Adherence and persistence outcomes were summarized and compared descriptively between injectable and oral GLP-1 RAs. Across the included total of 13 studies and medical records, data from 1348 patients were summarized. Oral GLP-1 RAs were associated with higher reported adherence (70.8% vs 62.4%) and persistence (62.1% vs 47.8%) compared with injectable formulations. A chi-square test of independence showed that the difference in adherence between oral and injectable GLP-1 was significant; (χ 2 = 10.8, p < 0.01). Similarly, chi-square test showed that the observed variation in persistence between Oral-GLP vs injectable GLP-1 was also significant (χ 2 = 37.9, p < 0.001). Injectable therapies were associated with higher rates of adverse events, particularly injection-site reactions. Oral GLP-1 RAs may be associated with improved adherence and persistence in patients with T2DM. These findings suggest that formulation choice may influence long-term diabetes treatment continuation, although further study-level meta-analytic research is needed.

title: Four Pillars in Type 2 Diabetes and Chronic Kidney Disease G4-G5: Mission Impossible-or Not Too Late to Start?
abstract: The 4-pillar therapy-renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, the nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist finerenone, and glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists-is increasingly applied to improve kidney and cardiovascular outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, landmark trials underpinning current recommendations largely enrolled participants down to estimated glomerular filtration rate thresholds of ∼20-30 mL/min/1.73 m2, leaving uncertainty in CKD G4-G5. This uncertainty contributes to an implementation gap in advanced CKD, which is as follows: missing pillars are often not initiated, therapies are interrupted during clinical complications, and they are not reinitiated once acute triggers resolve despite high absolute kidney and cardiovascular risk. This narrative review summarizes what current evidence does-and does not-support for initiating, continuing, temporarily withholding, discontinuing, and reinitiating each pillar in type 2 diabetes and CKD G4-G5. We integrate posthoc and subgroup analyses of landmark trials, meta-analyses, and pooled analyses, including low-estimated glomerular filtration rate strata and observational real-world data. The main practical message is that current evidence generally supports a monitoring-based approach to 4-pillar therapy in CKD G4, whereas decisions in CKD G5 remain more individualized and explicitly extrapolative. For clinicians, the key priority is to identify missing pillars, avoid unnecessary permanent discontinuation, and use structured reinitiation when clinically appropriate.

title: Real-World Anthropometric Outcomes, Safety, and Use Patterns of GLP-1 and Dual GIP/GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Obesity and Glucose Metabolism Disorder: A Nationwide Multicentre Community Pharmacy Study.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have transformed the management of obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Although randomized clinical trials have demonstrated substantial weight loss and metabolic benefits with incretin-based therapies, real-world evidence is needed to characterize anthropometric outcomes, safety, prescribing patterns, and treatment use under routine clinical conditions. The objective of this study was to characterize real-world anthropometric outcomes, safety, and use patterns of GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with obesity or glucose metabolism disorder receiving treatment through Spanish community pharmacies. A nationwide multicentre cross-sectional study with retrospective data collection was conducted between January and April 2026 across community pharmacies in Spain. Adult patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists or dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists were consecutively enrolled and classified according to therapeutic indication (obesity or glucose metabolism disorder). Changes in body weight and body mass index (BMI) were assessed using paired-sample t-tests, while multivariable linear regression explored independent determinants of weight loss. Crude safety signals were initially evaluated using exploratory crude safety association analysis based on Odds Ratios (ORs). Subsequently, multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors of suspected digestive adverse drug reactions after adjustment for demographic characteristics, treatment-related variables, lifestyle factors, and concomitant glucose-lowering therapies. Baseline body weight was retrospectively reported by participants and was not independently verified against clinical records or other objective sources, whereas current body weight was measured by the pharmacist at the study visit. A total of 531 patients were included (52.2% with obesity; 47.8% were classified in the glucose metabolism disorder (GMD) cohort, comprising 200 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and 54 with prediabetes/fasting glucose disturbance; the mean age was 56.5 ± 12.5 years; and 66.7% were women). The mean observed reduction in body weight from treatment initiation to the study assessment was 12.17 ± 10.64 kg, corresponding to an 11.71% ± 9.40% reduction relative to retrospectively reported baseline weight. Overall, 73.9% and 54.1% of participants achieved ≥5% and ≥10% weight loss, respectively. No statistically significant unadjusted difference in relative weight loss was detected across treatment groups; however, equivalence was not formally assessed. Gastrointestinal suspected adverse drug reactions were the most frequently reported safety outcomes. Exploratory crude analyses showed nominal associations between Wegovy® and nausea/vomiting and between Mounjaro® and constipation, as well as between concomitant insulin and dizziness and SGLT2 inhibitor therapy and urinary disorders; however, none of these associations remained statistically significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing. In the exploratory multivariable linear regression model, treatment duration, treatment agent, dietary adherence, light physical activity, and age showed statistically significant adjusted associations with observed percentage weight loss. In the multivariable logistic regression model, increasing age was the only variable significantly associated with lower odds of reported suspected digestive adverse drug reactions (adjusted OR = 0.97 per year; 95% CI 0.96-0.99; p = 0.003). Observed percentage weight loss varied across treatment groups, although between-treatment comparisons should be interpreted cautiously because of differences in treatment duration, therapeutic indication, sample size, and dose exposure. Given the retrospective ascertainment of baseline weight and the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as real-world estimates of observed weight change rather than causal estimates of treatment effectiveness. Reported suspected adverse drug reactions were common, particularly gastrointestinal events. Although several nominal associations were observed in exploratory crude analyses, none remained statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. These findings support the importance of individualized monitoring in community pharmacy settings. These findings provide a rationale for the prospective development and evaluation of a standardized pharmacy-led dispensing and follow-up protocol to support patient safety and treatment adherence.

title: Clinical Feasibility of a Low-Dose Tirzepatide Strategy in Older Adults with Type 2 Diabetes: Persistence, Metabolic Benefit, and Treatment Simplification in a Real-World Cohort.
journal: Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists
abstract: To evaluate the clinical feasibility of a low-dose tirzepatide strategy in older adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus in routine outpatient practice. This single-center retrospective cohort included Japanese adults who initiated tirzepatide between April 2024 and December 2025 and received a maximum observed dose of ≤5 mg/week through week 28. The primary endpoint in adults aged ≥65 years combined treatment persistence, absence of adverse event (AE)-related discontinuation, and either ≥3% weight loss or an HbA1c reduction ≥1.0 percentage point (≥11 mmol/mol). Younger adults were contextual comparators using overlap weighting. Among 122 tirzepatide initiators, 107 were included in the low-dose strategy cohort, including 37 older adults. The primary endpoint was achieved by 23/37 (62.2%); 33/37 (89.2%) remained on treatment, and 2/37 (5.4%) discontinued because of AEs. Median body weight change was -3.07%, median HbA1c change was -1.0 percentage point (-11 mmol/mol), and 19/37 (51.4%) achieved HbA1c <7.0% (<53 mmol/mol). Renal, hydration, and nutritional laboratory markers remained generally stable. Overlap-weighted comparisons showed no clear age-related attenuation. In selected older adults, low-dose tirzepatide provided modest metabolic benefit with high persistence and infrequent AE-related discontinuation.

title: Advances in disease management and treatment outcomes for obesity and knee osteoarthritis in primary care practice.
abstract: The lifetime risk of developing knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is approximately doubled in people with obesity compared with those without obesity. Many patients with KOA are treated by primary care physicians in the community setting. We performed a targeted literature search on PubMed to identify relevant literature describing the impact of weight loss in patients with obesity and KOA. A strong body of evidence supports the use of weight loss through lifestyle interventions, including caloric restriction in combination with exercise, as a primary intervention in patients with KOA and obesity. Studies show that these interventions are associated with improvements in pain, physical function, and quality of life; however, adherence to lifestyle interventions can be challenging, even with individually tailored programs. Obesity medications, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, are emerging as a new addition to weight management approaches in KOA, with a recent phase 3 clinical study demonstrating the benefits of semaglutide for weight loss in adults with KOA and high body mass index. Although initial data are promising, further clinical evidence is required, and perceived barriers to use need to be addressed before obesity medications can be widely adopted into clinical practice for patients with KOA. Specifically, further data are required to guide decisions regarding optimal treatment duration with obesity medications and to establish their tolerability profile associated with longer-term use. The importance of preserving functional muscle mass in patients with KOA and mitigation of weight regain after obesity medication treatment withdrawal are also identified as areas warranting further research. In this narrative review, we provide practical recommendations to primary care physicians on integrating obesity medications into weight-loss programs, including patient screening, risk stratification, communication, use of guidelines, and the benefits of a multidisciplinary approach.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and hair loss: adverse effect, epiphenomenon, or therapeutic paradox?
abstract: Incretin-based therapies, including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and dual/triple agonists, have revolutionized the management of obesity and type 2 diabetes. However, hair loss has emerged as an adverse event in clinical practice. This review synthesizes the evidence on the prevalence, mechanistic pathways, and clinical course of hair loss associated with semaglutide, tirzepatide, and retatrutide. A narrative review was conducted using the PubMed/MEDLINE database. Data were integrated from clinical trials, real-world observational studies, and pharmacovigilance databases to evaluate the oncological and dermatological implications of these therapies. There is a discrepancy in hair loss prevalence, ranging from 3 to 7% in controlled trials to over 70% in real-world cohorts. Telogen effluvium (TE) is the predominant phenotype, driven primarily by the magnitude and velocity of weight loss rather than drug toxicity. Newer agents like tirzepatide demonstrate stronger associations with hair shedding compared to older GLP-1 RAs. Pharmacovigilance data show inconsistent but significant signals for semaglutide and tirzepatide, with reporting odds ratios indicating a drug-associated risk. Conversely, paradoxical improvements in androgenetic alopecia and inflammatory scarring alopecias have been reported, likely mediated by metabolic normalization and anti-inflammatory effects. Female sex and significant weight reduction (> 10%) were the most robust predictors of hair loss. Hair loss associated with incretin-based therapies is a biologically complex, threshold-dependent phenomenon reflecting systemic metabolic reprogramming. While predominantly transient and reversible, its psychological impact can compromise treatment adherence. Clinicians should provide proactive counseling, emphasizing the self-limiting nature of TE in this context while monitoring for diverse follicular responses.

title: Obesity: oral therapy for those afraid of needles.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) pharmacotherapy has transformed obesity management, yet subcutaneous administration remains a barrier for patients with needle phobia. This review examines needle phobia and agoraphobia as contributors to treatment non-adherence and evaluates the evidence for oral GLP-1 RA alternatives. We synthesize evidence on the epidemiology of needle phobia (trypanophobia) and agoraphobia, their mechanisms and psychiatric comorbidities, real-world discontinuation rates of injectable GLP-1 RAs, and clinical efficacy data for oral semaglutide and emerging oral agents. A brief overview of the literature search methodology (PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, ClinicalTrials.gov; searched to June 2026) is provided in the Introduction. A structured clinical decision algorithm is proposed. Oral semaglutide 25 mg/day (the currently approved dose for weight management) demonstrates weight loss of similar magnitude to subcutaneous formulations across separate trials and should be considered preferentially in patients with moderate-to-severe needle phobia. Systematic needle phobia screening at obesity clinic entry, combined with a severity-based treatment algorithm integrating pharmacological and psychological approaches, is recommended to maximize equitable access to obesity pharmacotherapy.

title: Efsubaglutide Alfa: A Comprehensive Pharmacological Review.
abstract: Efsubaglutide alfa (also known as supaglutide) is a long-acting glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) engineered as a GLP-1 analogue fused to a human immunoglobulin G2 (IgG2) fragment crystallisable (Fc) domain. This narrative review summarises published and publicly available evidence on efsubaglutide alfa pharmacology, pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, dose-exposure-response relationships, drug-drug interaction potential, and clinical efficacy and safety in type 2 diabetes (T2D) and overweight/obesity. Efsubaglutide alfa has prolonged exposure (terminal half-life approximately 182-215 h) and low steady-state fluctuation, but dosing-interval selection should not be inferred from half-life alone. Available population pharmacokinetic and exposure-response analyses indicate that steady-state trough concentration is most informative for glycaemic response, whereas average and peak concentrations contribute to interpretation of weight response and gastrointestinal tolerability. Across available studies, predominantly conducted in Chinese populations, efsubaglutide alfa shows class-consistent improvements in glycaemic control and body weight, with gastrointestinal adverse events as the main tolerability limitation. Exploratory every 2-week dosing and post-discontinuation glycaemic durability findings remain hypothesis-generating. No head-to-head comparative trials dedicated cardiovascular or renal outcome trials, or large globally diverse datasets are yet available; therefore, the current evidence should be interpreted as a clinical pharmacology synthesis rather than a comparative positioning claim.

title: Nurse Practitioner-Led Integration of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Patients With Obesity-Related Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Prospective Clinical Effectiveness Study.
abstract: Obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is characterized by systemic inflammation and reduced functional capacity. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) improve symptoms and weight in randomized trials, but uptake in routine cardiovascular practice is inconsistent. The purpose of this study was to evaluate a structured nurse practitioner-led program for GLP-1 RA initiation in obesity-related HFpEF. Prospective 12-month, single-center pre-post effectiveness study at a U.S. urban academic outpatient cardiology clinic. Adults with left ventricular ejection fraction ≥45%, body mass index ≥30 kg/m2, New York Heart Association class II-III symptoms, and at least 1 cardiometabolic comorbidity were enrolled. The intervention included registry-based identification, baseline assessment, patient education, protocolized titration, and longitudinal follow-up. Each participant's 12-month preenrollment period served as a comparator. The primary outcome was GLP-1 RA initiation and 12-month persistence. Of 156 enrolled, 128 (82.1%) completed follow-up. Mean age 67.4 ± 11.2 years; 61.7% female; 43.8% Black. GLP-1 RA use rose from 7.8% to 92.2% (87.5% at target dose). Mean weight decreased 6.2 ± 3.8 kg, Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score improved 16.6 ± 11.3 points, and 6-minute walk distance rose 48.3 ± 36.2 m (all P < .001). Systolic blood pressure, hemoglobin A1c (diabetic subgroup), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide all decreased significantly. Heart failure hospitalization fell from 18.2% to 4.7% (P = .002). Gastrointestinal symptoms were most common; 4.7% discontinued for intolerance. A structured nurse practitioner-led cardiometabolic program was associated with high GLP-1 RA initiation and persistence and with clinically meaningful improvements in symptoms, function, and hospitalization in obesity-related HFpEF.

title: Weight Maintenance Following Discontinuation of Semaglutide in an Adolescent with Antipsychotic-Associated Weight Gain: A Case Report.
abstract: Antipsychotic-induced weight gain (AIWG) presents a significant clinical challenge in pediatric psychiatry, often leading to Class II or III obesity and metabolic comorbidities. While treatment with metformin is the current standard of care, its efficacy is often modest. Preclinical and translational data suggest that, by targeting the underlying cause of AIWG, GLP-1Ras may help restore satiety signaling that is disrupted in patients taking antipsychotics. We describe an adolescent who experienced profound weight gain following aripiprazole treatment which was successfully managed with semaglutide. Notably, after achieving therapeutic goals of normalization of body mass index (BMI) and hemoglobin A1c, the patient was able to discontinue semaglutide while maintaining her weight loss and normalization of hemoglobin A1c over six months of follow-up. This single case raises the hypothesis that GLP-1RAs could serve as a temporary "bridge therapy" to counteract iatrogenic metabolic insults; given the confounding factors discussed below, this observation is hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation in larger, prospective studies before broader clinical application.

title: Rethinking Obstructive Sleep Apnea Care in Obesity: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure, Incretin-Based Therapy, or Both?
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity
abstract: Obesity is a primary driver of obstructive sleep apnea and contributes substantially to its associated cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Although continuous positive airway pressure remains the standard treatment, its efficacy is often limited by suboptimal patient adherence and its impact on cardiovascular outcomes has yet to be consistently established in major clinical trials. Treatments aimed at the underlying problem, excess adiposity, are therefore needed. Weight loss, whether achieved through lifestyle interventions or bariatric surgery is well-known to improve obstructive sleep apnea. The recent introduction of highly effective weight loss medications, most notably incretin-based agents, now offers a pharmacological approach to accomplish the same result. Recent randomized controlled trials in patients with obesity demonstrated that these medications significantly decrease the apnea-hypopnea index and enhance oxygen saturation, with a significant proportion of disease remission. In light of these findings, we propose a therapeutic algorithm stratifying treatment according to symptoms and body mass index. For asymptomatic patients with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea, we suggest incretin-based therapy as a first-line option to concurrently address excessive weight and obstructive sleep apnea. Conversely, in individuals with impaired sleep-related quality of life combining continuous positive airway pressure and incretin therapy may be more appropriate, pairing immediate symptom control with longer-term weight loss. This integrated strategy, prioritizing weight management alongside symptom relief, may offer a comprehensive approach to treat obesity-related obstructive sleep apnea and decrease its associated cardiovascular risks.

title: Severe Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis After Semaglutide-Associated Poor Intake Despite Empagliflozin Discontinuation: A Case Report.
abstract: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (EDKA) may be overlooked when serum glucose is near normal. A 68-year-old woman with long-standing type 2 diabetes developed approximately three weeks of nausea, intermittent vomiting and diarrhea, and minimal oral intake after semaglutide initiation at 0.25 mg once weekly for four weeks followed by 0.5 mg once weekly. Patient and family medication reconciliation indicated that she had stopped empagliflozin, metformin, and pioglitazone approximately two weeks before presentation but continued semaglutide, with the last dose approximately eight days before admission. She presented with weakness, dyspnea, slowed speech, and disorientation. Initial testing showed glucose 132 mg/dL, venous pH 7.13, bicarbonate 9 mmol/L, anion gap 26 mmol/L, and beta-hydroxybutyrate 99.5 mg/dL. She improved with intravenous crystalloid, dextrose-containing fluids, insulin infusion, and electrolyte replacement. The temporal association is consistent with a clinically plausible contribution from semaglutide-associated gastrointestinal intolerance and carbohydrate depletion to EDKA despite reported prior empagliflozin discontinuation. Normal glucose should not delay ketone and acid-base testing when compatible symptoms and poor intake are present.

title: Tirzepatide-induced pneumatosis intestinalis: a rare but clinically significant gastrointestinal adverse effect.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists such as tirzepatide are increasingly prescribed to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity because they improve glycemic control and promote weight loss. Although gastrointestinal adverse effects such as nausea, vomiting, constipation, and delayed gastric emptying are well recognized, very rare cases of pneumatosis intestinalis have also been reported in association with this class of medications. We report the first documented histologic diagnosis of a possible tirzepatide-associated pneumatosis intestinalis. A 55-year-old man with obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnea underwent colonoscopy for evaluation of abdominal pain, constipation, and anal fissures. He had been receiving tirzepatide therapy for approximately 1 year and experienced a 49-pound weight loss. Colonoscopy demonstrated mucosal edema of the cecum and ascending colon. Biopsy specimens of the colon revealed mucosal and submucosal air-filled spaces associated with foreign body-type giant cell reactions and mixed inflammatory infiltrates, including eosinophils and neutrophils, consistent with pneumatosis intestinalis. The patient lacked other recognized risk factors for pneumatosis intestinalis, and his symptoms improved following discontinuation of tirzepatide. As the use of tirzepatide and related glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists continues to increase, awareness of this rare side effect and its characteristic histologic features should facilitate prompt recognition and accurate diagnosis. Reporting these rare events remains essential to refine the safety profile of these increasingly used medications and improve our understanding of their long-term gastrointestinal effects in broader patient populations.

title: Real-world treatment-transition pathways and dosing patterns of insulin degludec/liraglutide in Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes.
abstract: To describe real-world treatment-transition pathways, early IDegLira dosing patterns, treatment simplification, and observed short-term clinical outcomes among Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D). This multicenter, non-interventional, retrospective observational registry included 1499 adults with T2D who initiated IDegLira in routine practice across 13 provinces and regions in China from April 2022 to December 2023. The five mutually exclusive prior-treatment pathways were non-injectable therapy, basal insulin, multiple daily injections (MDI), insulin plus GLP-1RA, and GLP-1RA-based therapy. Treatment decisions were physician-directed. Eligible patients had documented continuous use of once-daily IDegLira (the fixed-ratio combination [FRC]) for at least 3 months. Early dosing was defined as the starting dose, dose titration, and dose documented at approximately 12 weeks. Exploratory linear models estimated crude and covariate-adjusted between-pathway differences in paired HbA1c and body-weight change. Baseline HbA1c was available for 1374 patients (9.05 ± 1.78%) and week-12 HbA1c for 498 patients (7.44 ± 2.29%). Among 480 patients with paired baseline and week-12 HbA1c data (all enrolled in the final study period), mean HbA1c decreased from 9.11 ± 2.09% to 7.45 ± 2.28% (mean change -1.66 ± 2.23 percentage points; P < 0.001). Among the week-12 evaluable population, 21.08%, 47.39%, 81.73%, and 89.36% had HbA1c ≤ 6.5%, <7.0%, <7.5%, and <8.0%, respectively. Among 487 patients with paired baseline and week-12 body-weight data (all from the final study period), mean body weight decreased from 75.48 ± 11.12 to 72.72 ± 10.56 kg (mean change -2.76 ± 4.93 kg). In exploratory adjusted models, HbA1c reductions were smaller after basal insulin (mean difference +0.82 percentage points, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.27) and MDI (+1.25, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.98) than after non-injectable therapy, whereas no overall adjusted pathway association was observed for body-weight change (global P = 0.606). The mean starting dose was 14.46 ± 4.06 U and the mean week-12/current dose was 16.72 ± 4.55 U among available cases. Prandial insulin discontinuation was recorded in 269/301 MDI patients (89.37%); concurrent paired HbA1c and systematic post-initiation safety data were unavailable for this subgroup. This study describes real-world treatment-transition and dosing patterns for IDegLira across heterogeneous prior therapies. Glycemic findings are based on the week-12 evaluable population (498 of 1499 patients, all enrolled in the final study period); among 480 patients with paired baseline and week-12 HbA1c data, mean HbA1c decreased by 1.66 percentage points. The study had no comparator group and no basis for causal inference. The findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, and may inform clinical discussions and future comparative studies.

title: Tirzepatide persistence, adherence, and dose escalation in a real-world setting with high out-of-pocket costs: a Polish cohort study.
abstract: Tirzepatide is effective in clinical trials, but its real-world use where obesity pharmacotherapy is self-funded remains poorly characterized. We aimed to characterize tirzepatide persistence, adherence, and dose escalation in a high out-of-pocket-cost setting. We retrospectively analyzed nationwide electronic health records from a large Polish private healthcare provider. We included 3030 adults with a first recorded tirzepatide prescription between November 2023 and February 2025. The primary endpoint was time to observed treatment discontinuation. Multivariable Cox regression identified persistence predictors, while adherence was assessed using proportion of days covered (PDC). Successful titration was escalation from 2.5 or 5 mg to ≥10 mg. The cohort included 69.0% women; 83.3% had obesity and 20.0% had type 2 diabetes. Higher first recorded dose was associated with earlier loss of observed treatment. Compared with 2.5 mg initiators, the hazard ratio for discontinuation was 1.44 (95%CI 1.26-1.64, p < 0.001) for 15 mg and 1.24 (95%CI 1.12-1.39, p < 0.001) for 10 mg doses. Traditional comorbidities did not independently predict persistence (all p > 0.10). Among385 patients persistent for ≥180 days, median PDC was 0.86 (IQR 0.73-0.95), with 68% classified as adherent (PDC ≥80%). Of 2194 eligible low-dose patients, 565 (25.8%) escalated to ≥10 mg, corresponding to 18.6% of the full cohort. Real-world tirzepatide persistence was suboptimal and associated with recorded starting dose. Traditional clinical comorbidities had limited impact on discontinuation timing. Nonclinical factors, including affordability, tolerability, and patient expectations, may contribute to early loss of observed treatment; although these were not directly measured.

title: A stewardship framework for incretin-based therapies in weight management.
journal: Journal of the American Pharmacists Association : JAPhA
abstract: Use of incretin-based therapies, including GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonists, for weight management and related cardio-kidney-liver-metabolic comorbidities has expanded rapidly, yet real-world practice is challenged by inconsistent prescribing, access barriers, limited long-term safety data, low treatment persistence, and concerns regarding equity and financial sustainability. These gaps highlight the need for a structured, coordinated stewardship model to guide safe and evidence-based use of incretin-based therapies. To develop a scalable, multidisciplinary stewardship framework for incretin-based therapies that supports consistent and efficient prescribing practices, optimizes patient outcomes, strengthens medication access and safety monitoring, and defines the role of pharmacists in chronic weight management. Two sequential expert workgroups were convened, composed of clinicians and pharmacy leaders from 21 health systems. Workgroup 1 identified foundational stewardship elements drawing from established antimicrobial and opioid stewardship models. Workgroup 2 applied these core principles to incretin-based therapies, informed by real-world challenges, emerging evidence, and clinical experience in weight and diabetes management. Consensus was established using a Delphi process, with ≥60% agreement required for inclusion. Workgroups reached consensus on a stewardship framework comprising multidisciplinary leadership, stakeholder engagement, pharmacy expertise, defined priorities, evidence-based interventions, education, data and reporting strategies, communication pathways, and mechanisms for feedback and continuous assessment. In addition, consensus-based pharmacist-led initiatives and metric categories were developed to support implementation and program evaluation across varied ambulatory environments, with pharmacists identified as central to therapy initiation and titration, adverse effect management, access navigation, patient education, and care coordination. A structured stewardship model offers a feasible and scalable approach to optimize incretin-based therapies in weight management. By integrating multidisciplinary collaboration with pharmacy expertise and clinical and operational strategies, health systems can promote safe, equitable, and sustainable use of these therapies, improve population-level outcomes, and safeguard long-term value amid rapidly expanding utilization.

title: The PTPN1/N2 Peptide Inhibitor Achieves Potent, Long-Acting Glycemic Control and Weight-Loss Dual Efficacy in Mice.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity are closely linked metabolic disorders driven by insulin and leptin resistance. Current long-acting therapies capable of addressing both conditions are dominated by incretin-based agents, which primarily achieve efficacy through appetite suppression and are frequently associated with tolerability limitations and metabolic rebound after treatment discontinuation. Alternative strategies that correct underlying signaling defects without suppressing food intake remain lacking. Protein tyrosine phosphatases PTPN1 and PTPN2 act as coordinated intracellular negative regulators of insulin and leptin signaling by dephosphorylating key molecules within the IRS-AKT and JAK2-STAT3 pathways. Although genetic studies have established these phosphatases as attractive therapeutic targets, translation has been hindered by the absence of long-acting inhibitors with robust in vivo efficacy. Here we report the rational design of Y5, a chemically engineered BimBH3-derived peptide analogue that functions as a dual inhibitor of PTPN1 and PTPN2. Fatty-acid conjugation and hapten modification confer high enzymatic potency, enhanced proteolytic stability, strong albumin binding, and prolonged half-life and systemic exposure. Y5 restores cellular insulin and leptin signaling in vitro, leading to coordinated activation of IRS-1, AKT, and STAT3 under resistant conditions. In diabetic db/db mice, Y5 once-weekly administration induces sustained glycemic control, improves glucose tolerance, and reduces circulating insulin levels, consistent with enhanced insulin sensitivity. In DIO mice, Y5 induces pronounced and sustained weight loss while preserving food intake, demonstrating a potential mechanism distinct from incretin-based therapies. Y5 selectively reduces adiposity, improves hepatic steatosis, and is well tolerated across dosing regimens. These findings establish long-acting dual inhibition of PTPN1 and PTPN2 as a mechanistically distinct therapeutic strategy for T2DM and obesity. By reversing hormone resistance rather than suppressing appetite, Y5 defines an alternative paradigm for achieving long-acting glycemic control and weight loss in vivo.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy for Glucocorticoid-Induced Dysglycaemia: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Glucocorticoids (GCs) commonly induce glycaemic disturbance, from transient steroid-induced hyperglycaemia to steroid-induced diabetes and contribute to post-transplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM). Insulin remains the standard treatment for GC-induced glycaemic dysregulation. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have a mechanistic rationale here, but their efficacy and safety in GC-induced dysglycaemia have not been systematically appraised. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines (registration number: CRD420251183082). Embase, PubMed/MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched up to May 2026. A structured narrative synthesis was the primary method. Thirteen studies were included, predominantly retrospective cohort studies; 10 enrolled solid organ transplant recipients with PTDM or pre-existing type 2 diabetes. GLP-1 RA therapy, either as monotherapy or as an adjunct to insulin, was associated with reductions in HbA1c and body weight, and a low rate of hypoglycaemia in the majority of included studies. GLP-1 RAs led to insulin dose reduction or discontinuation, reducing injection frequency and treatment burden. Five studies contributed to at least one pooled estimate, and no outcome was informed by more than three studies; given substantial heterogeneity and very low GRADE certainty, these estimates are exploratory and are presented in Supplementary Material 2. Individual studies reported reductions in HbA1c, body weight and insulin dose, with a low rate of hypoglycaemia episodes. However, available data specific to GC-induced dysglycaemia remain insufficient. Prospective controlled trials with explicit characterisation of GC exposure are required.

title: GLP-1 receptor biology and the therapeutic role of incretin-based agonists in metabolic diseases.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2DM) and obesity represent a growing global health burden, sharing underlying pathophysiological mechanisms such as impaired insulin signalling and chronic low-grade inflammation. The discovery of the incretin effect opened the way for agonist therapies targeting the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) as therapies capable of addressing the metabolic dysregulation common to both diseases simultaneously. This review examines the biology of GLP-1 and the incretin system, with a focus on the structure and signalling mechanisms of GLP-1R, including biased agonism and receptor trafficking. The clinical effectiveness of stable, long-acting GLP-1RAs is evaluated across three therapeutic domains: T2DM management, obesity treatment, and emerging cardiovascular protection. Current evidence demonstrates that GLP-1RAs, which induce insulin secretion and suppress appetite, achieve superior glycaemic control and significant weight reduction compared with conventional therapies, with emerging cardiovascular benefits now extending to non-diabetic patients as well. The shift towards dual and triple receptor agonists, such as tirzepatide and retatrutide, together with biased agonist design, is a promising development for further improvements in effectiveness. Progress in oral formulations of GLP-1RAs may also improve tolerability and patient adherence. Nevertheless, important challenges remain, including gastrointestinal side effects, weight regain upon discontinuation, loss of lean body mass, and unresolved questions regarding long-term safety. In conclusion, while GLP-1R-based therapies represent a major therapeutic advancement, particularly for T2DM patients, their broader application in obesity management requires careful patient selection, continued long-term safety monitoring, and integration with lifestyle interventions.

title: Ischemic colitis associated with oral semaglutide with recurrence upon rechallenge.
abstract: Ischemic colitis associated with glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists is an exceptionally rare condition, with only a few cases reported in the literature. We present the case of a 46-year-old woman treated with oral semaglutide (Rybelsus®) for weight loss who experienced three episodes of abdominal pain and hematochezia temporally associated with drug exposure. The third episode, which occurred after semaglutide was reintroduced, led to a confirmed diagnosis based on computed tomography, rectosigmoidoscopy, and histopathological findings consistent with ischemic colitis. Permanent discontinuation of semaglutide was followed by complete clinical resolution without further recurrence. The temporal relationship, improvement after drug withdrawal, and recurrence upon rechallenge support a probable causal association. This case highlights the need to consider ischemic colitis as a potential rare adverse effect of semaglutide.

title: Preventing Weight Regain After Glucagon-Like Peptide‑1 Therapy Discontinuation: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are effective treatments for obesity, but discontinuation is common due to cost, insurance coverage limitations, side effects, patient preference, and other factors. Weight regain often occurs rapidly after cessation, yet few evidence-based strategies exist to support weight maintenance during this transition. This pilot randomized trial examined whether a digital wellness application or medically tailored meals (MTM) could mitigate weight gain during the first 4 months after GLP-1 cessation. In this pilot randomized trial, adults with prior GLP-1-induced weight loss were randomized to usual care, wellness application, or MTM at the time of GLP-1 cessation. Surveys assessed adherence and satisfaction (primary outcome) as well as exploratory outcomes, diet quality, and perceived health. Weight (exploratory) was measured monthly using validated Bluetooth scales. Participants (n = 39) were randomized to control (N = 14), digital wellness application (N = 12), or MTM (N = 13) and had a mean baseline BMI 31.4 (SD 6.3) kg/m2. Diet quality, perceived health, adherence, and satisfaction did not significantly differ by group, though some estimates suggested possible trends favoring the wellness application. Relative to control, both the wellness application and MTM groups had less total weight gain: Wellness application -7.16% (95% CI: -12.27, -2.04) and MTM -7.17% (-12.20, -2.14). These findings suggest that structured support may attenuate early weight gain after GLP-1 cessation. Larger, more diverse trials with longer follow-up and clinical outcomes are needed to confirm results and clarify mechanisms.

title: Oral small-molecule GLP-1RA safiglipron versus dapagliflozin in type 2 diabetes: a randomized, double-blind, active-comparator-controlled phase 3 trial.
abstract: Safiglipron is an oral small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist administered without fasting or dietary restrictions. We evaluated its efficacy and safety versus dapagliflozin in OUTSTAND-2, a phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-comparator-controlled trial conducted at 98 sites in China. We randomized 810 adults (mean hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) 8.60%, median diabetes duration 5.0 years, 35.7% women) to safiglipron 30 mg (n = 202), safiglipron 60 mg (n = 203), safiglipron 90 mg (n = 203) or dapagliflozin 10 mg (n = 202) for 32 weeks, followed by a 20-week active-treatment extension. For the primary endpoint, treatment differences versus dapagliflozin in change from baseline in HbA1c at week 32 under the primary non-inferiority estimand were -0.30% (95% confidence interval (CI): -0.51 to -0.09), -0.22% (-0.44 to -0.01) and -0.40% (-0.62 to -0.19) for safiglipron 30 mg, 60 mg and 90 mg, respectively, establishing non-inferiority for all three doses (all P < 0.0001; non-inferiority margin 0.4%). Under the treatment policy estimand, 90 mg met the prespecified statistical criterion for superiority (difference -0.25%; 95% CI: -0.45 to -0.05; one-sided P = 0.0067), whereas 60 mg did not (P = 0.0789), after which fixed-sequence testing stopped. HbA1c target attainment rates with safiglipron versus dapagliflozin were 54.9-63.5% versus 36.5% for HbA1c <7.0% and 38.9-48.6% versus 16.1% for HbA1c ≤6.5%. Mean body weight changes were -2.35%, -3.55%, -4.17% and -3.60% for safiglipron 30 mg, safiglipron 60 mg, safiglipron 90 mg and dapagliflozin, respectively. Fasting plasma glucose, seven-point self-monitored blood glucose profiles, waist circumference, HOMA-β, HOMA-IR and changes in treatment satisfaction showed varying degrees of improvement from baseline with both safiglipron and dapagliflozin. Rescue therapy was used by 0.5-1.5% versus 0% of participants, respectively. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with safiglipron and mostly mild or moderate; adverse events led to treatment discontinuation in 4.0%, 4.0%, 3.9% and 1.5% of participants, respectively. Safiglipron provides an effective oral treatment option for adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with metformin. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06589765 .

title: Biologic Injection-Related Pain in Severe Asthma, Its Impact on Treatment Aversion, and Pain-Relief Approach: A Multicenter Observational Study.
journal: The journal of allergy and clinical immunology. In practice
abstract: Although biologic therapies are essential for managing severe asthma, injection-related pain may be a frequently overlooked barrier to treatment persistence. To quantify biologic injection-related pain in asthma cases, identify clinical factors associated with such pain and treatment aversion, and explore practical pain-relief approaches. This multicenter observational study enrolled patients with asthma receiving biologics between May 2025 and March 2026. Insertion pain, injection pain, and treatment aversion attributable to injection-related pain were assessed using 0 to 10 visual analog scales. Associations between clinical factors, pain scores, and treatment aversion scores and the effects of local pressure and cooling at the injection site were evaluated. Patients with diabetes mellitus receiving tirzepatide served as a reference group. In total, 122 biologic-treated and 27 tirzepatide-treated patient responses were analyzed. Mean insertion and injection pain scores for biologics were 3.00 ± 2.60 and 3.28 ± 2.91, respectively. Adjusted pain scores did not differ significantly across biologics and tirzepatide. Insertion pain was associated with anxiety and arm injection, whereas injection pain was associated with younger age and female sex. Both insertion and injection pain showed independent associations with log-transformed treatment aversion score (unstandardized regression coefficient [B] = 0.08, 95% CI, 0.03-0.12, and B = 0.07, 95% CI, 0.03-0.11, respectively). Injection-site cooling significantly reduced both pain types. Among patients receiving biologics for asthma, injection-related pain is common and independently associated with treatment aversion. Local cooling may offer a simple approach to reducing injection-related pain and addressing treatment aversion.

title: Real-World Adherence Patterns and Predictors of GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use for Obesity Management in a Medicaid Population.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have emerged as effective anti-obesity medications (AOMs); however, real-world adherence and persistence patterns among Medicaid populations remain poorly understood, specifically after medication shortage resolution. This study examined adherence and persistence to GLP-1 RA AOMs among Mississippi (MS) Medicaid members following statewide coverage initiation in July 2023. This cohort study utilized MS Medicaid claims data from January 2023 to December 2025. Members aged ≥ 18 years initiating GLP-1 RA AOMs between July 2023 and June 2025, with 6 months of continuous enrollment pre- and post-initiation, were included. Adherence rate was defined as percentage of members with proportion of days covered (PDC) greater than 0.8, and persistence rate was defined as percentage of members with continuous therapy without a 60-day gap, evaluated at 3- and 6-month intervals. Group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) identified distinct adherence trajectories, and multinomial logistic regression assessed predictors of trajectory membership. A subgroup analysis was conducted for members initiating between July 2023 and December 2024, who had 12-month follow-up period. The final analytic cohort included 3968 members, predominantly female (92.52%), Black (50.28%), and younger adults (18-39 years; 61.95%). Adherence rates declined from 56.85% at 3 months to 38.16% at 6 months, with persistence rates decreasing from 72.98% to 51.03% over the same period. In the 12-month subgroup analysis, adherence and persistence rates declined to 25.26% and 36.67%, respectively. GBTM identified five trajectories: consistent adherent (52.27%), delayed decliner (13.53%), consistent decliner (12.85%), fluctuating adherent (11.14%), and rapid discontinuer (10.21%). Treatment initiation in 2023, younger age, Black race, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular comorbidities were associated with suboptimal adherence trajectories, while managed care organization enrollment and hypertension were protective. GLP-1 RA AOM adherence declines substantially over time among MS Medicaid members. Targeted interventions are needed to sustain long-term therapeutic engagement.

title: Survodutide for the treatment of obesity: Mechanistic rationale, clinical evidence, and remaining uncertainties.
abstract: Survodutide (BI 456906) is an investigational once-weekly dual glucagon and Glucagon-like Peptide (GLP-1) receptor agonist being developed for obesity. In a phase 2 trial involving adults with a body mass index ≥27 kg/m2 without diabetes, participants assigned to the 4.8-mg dose achieved a mean body-weight reduction of up to 18.7% at 46 weeks, compared with 2.3% with placebo. Its proposed mechanism combines reduced food intake through GLP-1 receptor agonism with glucagon receptor-mediated effects on energy expenditure and hepatic metabolism. Gastrointestinal adverse events, including nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, were common and were influenced by dose escalation. Phase 3 SYNCHRONIZE trials are evaluating efficacy, safety, and tolerability in broader populations with and without type 2 diabetes. Survodutide is not approved for routine clinical use, and its comparative effectiveness, durability, long-term safety, treatment persistence, and effects after discontinuation remain to be established.

title: Cardiovascular safety of orforglipron versus insulin glargine in adults with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk (ACHIEVE-4): a phase 3, event-driven, randomised, open-label, non-inferiority, active comparator trial.
abstract: Orforglipron is an oral, non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist. While some peptide GLP-1 receptor agonists have established cardiovascular benefit, the cardiovascular safety of non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonists has not been studied. This study aimed to compare the effect of orforglipron with insulin glargine on the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events in individuals with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight who are at increased risk for cardiovascular events. This event-driven, phase 3, multicentre, randomised, open-label, active comparator, parallel-group study was conducted in 317 sites across 16 countries and territories. Adults with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk with glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) concentrations between 7·0% and 10·5% (53-91 mmol/mol) and a BMI of 25 kg/m2 or more, treated with up to three glucose-lowering medications (metformin, a sulfonylurea, and/or an SGLT2 inhibitor), were randomly assigned (1:1) to oral orforglipron maximum tolerated dose (up to 36 mg capsule [equivalent to 17·2 mg tablet]) or injectable titrated insulin glargine, each administered once daily. All participants had established cardiovascular or chronic kidney disease. The primary outcome was time to occurrence of four-component major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE-4), including cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, or hospitalisation for unstable angina. Non-inferiority of orforglipron to insulin glargine was declared if the upper limit of the two-sided 95% CI for the hazard ratio (HR; orforglipron vs insulin glargine) was less than 1·8. The primary endpoint and other safety endpoints were assessed in all participants who took at least one dose of assigned treatment using all datapoints from baseline until withdrawal or study completion, regardless of treatment adherence. This trial was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05803421) and is completed. Between May 1, 2023, and Sept 5, 2024, 2749 participants were randomly assigned (1371 to orforglipron and 1378 to insulin glargine). 1032 (38%) participants were female and 1717 (62·5%) male. 2362 (85·9%) participants had established cardiovascular disease and 1033 (37·6%) had chronic kidney disease. Mean baseline age, HbA1c, and BMI were 63·1 years (SD 9·9), 8·2% (1·0), and 33 kg/m2 (6·2), respectively. Over a median follow-up of 2 years, the primary outcome occurred in 57 (4·2%) of 1358 orforglipron participants and 67 (5·0%) of 1343 insulin glargine participants, showing non-inferiority to insulin glargine for MACE-4 (HR 0·84; 95% CI 0·59-1·20; p<0·0001 for non-inferiority). Gastrointestinal adverse events were reported in 851 (62·1%) of 1371 orforglipron participants and 193 (14·2%) of 1355 insulin glargine participants; clinically significant or severe hypoglycaemia (glucose <3 mmol/L [54 mg/dL]) occurred in 93 (6·8%) of 1371 orforglipron participants and 260 (19·2%) of 1355 insulin glargine participants. 62 deaths were reported during the study: 19 (1·4%) of 1371 participants receiving orforglipron and 43 (3·2%) of 1355 participants receiving insulin glargine; all deaths except one (in the insulin glargine group) were deemed unrelated to treatment. In people with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk, the cardiovascular safety of orforglipron was confirmed by demonstrating non-inferiority to insulin glargine for MACE-4. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequent adverse event and most common reason for orforglipron treatment discontinuation with orforglipron, while clinically significant hypoglycaemia occurred less frequently with orforglipron than with insulin glargine. These findings support orforglipron as a potential once-daily, oral treatment option with established cardiovascular safety in people with type 2 diabetes and increased cardiovascular risk. Eli Lilly and Company.

title: Retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes (TRIUMPH-2): a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial.
abstract: Retatrutide is an agonist of GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors, and is currently under investigation for the treatment of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other comorbidities, including knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnoea. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes. TRIUMPH-2 was a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial conducted at 92 medical and research centres and hospitals across eight countries. We enrolled adults (aged ≥18 years) with a BMI of 27 kg/m2 or higher and type 2 diabetes (glycated haemoglobin [HbA1c] 6·5-10·5%) on stable treatment for type 2 diabetes for at least 90 days before screening (diet or exercise alone, or up to three oral glucose-lowering medications), and a history of at least one self-reported unsuccessful dietary effort to reduce bodyweight. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1), using an interactive web-response system, to receive once-weekly subcutaneous injections (self-administered) of placebo or retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg. The primary endpoint was the percentage change from baseline to week 80 in bodyweight for the retatrutide 9 mg and 12 mg doses versus placebo, with 4 mg versus placebo a key secondary endpoint. Efficacy analyses included all randomly assigned participants, with missing data imputed with a primary multiple imputation strategy for the treatment regimen estimand. Safety analyses included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of study drug. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05929079 (completed). Between July 11, 2023, and Nov 1, 2024, 2047 participants were screened, and 1152 (mean age 55·1 years [SD 10·8], 554 [48%] females and 598 [52%] males, and 672 [58%] of White ethnicity) were randomly assigned to retatrutide 4 mg (n=292), 9 mg (n=284), or 12 mg (n=287), or placebo (n=289). At baseline, the mean BMI was 38·2 kg/m2 (SD 7·4), mean HbA1c was 7·71% (1·07), median duration of obesity was 21 years (IQR 11-31), and median duration of diabetes was 5·6 years (2·6-10·4). At baseline, 1055 (92%) of 1152 participants were on any oral glucose-lowering medication, including biguanides, SGLT2 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, and other oral glucose-lowering medications. Of 1152 participants, 965 (84%) completed the study drug. For the treatment regimen estimand, the mean percentage change from baseline in bodyweight at week 80 was -11·9% (SE 0·6) with retatrutide 4 mg, -16·8% (0·7) with retatrutide 9 mg, -18·8% (0·7) with retatrutide 12 mg, and -5·1% (0·7) with placebo. Estimated treatment differences compared with placebo for percentage change in bodyweight were -6·9% (95% CI -8·7 to -5·1) with retatrutide 4 mg, -11·8% (-13·7 to -9·8) with retatrutide 9 mg, and -13·8% (-15·8 to -11·8) with retatrutide 12 mg (p<0·0001 for all). The most frequently reported adverse events were gastrointestinal, which were more common in the retatrutide groups than in the placebo group (diarrhoea occurred in 80 [27%] of 292 participants in the 4 mg group, 95 [34%] of 284 in the 9 mg group, and 96 [34%] of 286 in the 12 mg group vs 38 [13%] of 287 in the placebo group, and nausea occurred in 40 [14%], 59 [21%], and 80 [28%] vs 23 [8%]). Hypotension and dysesthesia were more frequent with retatrutide than with placebo (four [1%] in the 4 mg group, 14 [5%] in the 9 mg group, and 18 (6%) in the 12 mg group vs one [<1%] in the placebo group with hypotension; 13 [4%], 16 [6%], and 21 [7%] vs two [1%] in the placebo group with dysesthesia). Permanent treatment discontinuation due to adverse events or death was more frequent in participants treated with retatrutide 9 mg (33 [12%]) and 12 mg (22 [8%]) compared with retatrutide 4 mg (11 [4%]) and placebo (14 [5%]). Two participants died in the retatrutide 4 mg group, three in the 9 mg group, one in the 12 mg group, and one in the placebo group; all deaths were deemed to be unrelated to the study intervention by the investigator. Treatment with retatrutide resulted in substantial improvements in bodyweight and was associated with improvements in glycaemic control in participants with obesity and type 2 diabetes, with a safety profile generally consistent with other molecules with GLP-1 receptor agonism. These results show that retatrutide might be effective for the treatment of obesity in people with type 2 diabetes. Eli Lilly and Company.

title: Semaglutide for Treating Paediatric Craniopharyngioma-Related Obesity: A Multicentre Case Series.
abstract: Obesity is a complication of childhood craniopharyngioma that remains difficult to treat. We investigated whether semaglutide was associated with a decrease in BMI among adolescents with craniopharyngioma-related obesity. This multicentre retrospective study included 20 patients < 18 years old with craniopharyngioma and obesity (BMI > 2 WHO Z-score) from 2019 to 2024 (source population: 139 children with craniopharyngioma, including 36 children with obesity). They received off-label semaglutide with dose titration (0.25-2 mg/week), tailored to tolerance and clinical response. The primary outcome was the within-patient comparison of BMI change from -12 months to treatment initiation and from initiation to +12 months. At semaglutide initiation, patients were 14.0 ± 3.9 years old, the interval since craniopharyngioma diagnosis was 6.3 ± 4.7 years, and BMI was 33.4 ± 3.9 kg/m2 (3.2 ± 0.7 Z-score). Tumour treatment was surgery alone (8/20), surgery and proton therapy (11/20), or proton therapy alone (1/20). All patients had growth hormone and TSH deficiency; 19/20 had ACTH and AVP deficiency. In the year before treatment, patients gained 3.5 ± 4.4 kg/m2 in BMI and 0.6 ± 1.6 in BMI Z-score; after 1 year of semaglutide therapy, they lost 2.5 ± 3.9 kg/m2 in BMI and 0.5 ± 0.5 in BMI Z-score (paired comparisons, p < 0.001 and p = 0.004, respectively). During treatment, BMI decreased by 10% or more in 40% of patients (95% CI: 19%-64%). Gastrointestinal side effects occurred in 30% of patients but were mild. No cases of treatment discontinuation, pituitary insufficiency decompensation or tumour recurrence were observed. Semaglutide was associated with reversal of weight gain among adolescents with craniopharyngioma-related obesity.

title: Tirzepatide Initiation in Lithium-Treated Bipolar Disorder: Renal Biomarker Trajectories and Lithium Safety Signals Over 12 Months in a Real-World Cohort.
abstract: To assess early renal and lithium-related safety and 12-month renal biomarker trajectories after tirzepatide initiation in lithium-treated adults with bipolar disorder. We retrospectively studied 23 adults at one centre. The principal 12-week renal safety measures were serum creatinine and derived CKD-EPI 2021 creatinine-based eGFR. Secondary outcomes included lithium, electrolytes, gastrointestinal symptoms, acute kidney injury meeting KDIGO creatinine criteria and discontinuation. Twelve-month trajectories and body-surface-area-unindexed eGFR were exploratory. At 12 weeks, creatinine changed by -3 ± 12 μmol/L (p = 0.196), indexed eGFR by +2.6 ± 15.1 mL/min/1.73 m2 (p = 0.259) and lithium by +0.08 ± 0.17 mmol/L (p = 0.030). Among 20 on-treatment completers at 12 months, weight decreased by 17.7 ± 6.0%, creatinine by 12 ± 9 μmol/L, indexed eGFR increased by 13.0 ± 12.1 mL/min/1.73 m2 and unindexed eGFR by 4.5 ± 14.3 mL/min. Two patients had lithium > 1.2 mmol/L; one developed clinician-attributed symptomatic toxicity and discontinued tirzepatide. No acute kidney injury meeting KDIGO creatinine criteria could be confirmed from available records. Co-prescription warrants structured monitoring and sick-day education. Creatinine-based eGFR changes during major weight loss do not establish renal benefit or exclude kidney injury.

title: An RNA thermogenic therapy to preserve lean mass and enhance metabolic health during GLP-1 weight loss.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Current obesity therapies reduce weight but often fail to preserve lean mass or sustain metabolic benefit. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) improve obesity-associated metabolic disease, but weight loss is often accompanied by reduced energy expenditure, loss of lean mass, and rapid fat-predominant regain after treatment discontinuation. We hypothesized that pharmacologic activation of adipose thermogenesis could specifically target fat loss, complement appetite suppression by increasing energy expenditure, and improve the metabolic quality of weight loss. Guided by our finding that diet-induced thermogenesis is mediated by a zinc finger protein 423 (ZFP423)-controlled pathway, we developed adipose-directed antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting ZFP423, a transcriptional repressor of brown and beige adipocyte identity. In lean and diet-induced obese mice, weekly Zfp423 ASO treatment induced white adipose beiging, increased body temperature and oxygen consumption, and improved glucose homeostasis, insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial respiration, and hepatic steatosis. When combined with the GLP1-RA semaglutide, Zfp423 ASO produced greater weight and fat loss than either monotherapy while preserving lean mass and improving metabolic outcomes. These findings identify Zfp423 as an RNA therapeutic target and support adipose thermogenesis as a complementary strategy for metabolically healthier obesity treatment.

title: Considerations and challenges in microdosing of GLP-1-based receptor agonists.
abstract: This commentary summarizes the pharmacologic rationale, emerging evidence, clinical considerations, and limitations of microdosing glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-based therapies.
